items.title: One in four questions in Dutch parliament “written using AI”
items.summary: Around a quarter of questions from MPs in the Dutch parliament were written with the help of AI tools such...
items.body_text:
One in four questions in Dutch parliament “written using AI”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Around a quarter of questions from MPs in the Dutch parliament were written with the help of AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude, according to research by broadcaster NOS.
NOS analysed 28,000 questions using the AI detection tool Pangram and found that 26% of them showed stylistic features of AI.
Usage peaked at more than 30% just before the summer recess, but dropped to around 17% in July, roughly the same level as a year go.
Some MPs included a sentence or two of AI, while others used to generate whole strings of questions.
Last week prime minister Rob Jetten was criticised after it emerged that around 30% of his social media posts included AI-generated content.
Some of the messages were apparently personal reflections on sensitive subjects such as the mistreatment of Moluccan war veterans in the 1950s, which Jetten recently apologised for on behalf of the government.
Jetten defended the practice, saying that “like three-quarters of Dutch people I sometimes use AI to make things better”.
The use of AI to formulate questions is not necessarily a problem, according to some experts. “If MPs weren’t using it at all I would see that as a bad thing,” AI developer Maarten Sukel told NOS.
But he said it should not be used as a short-cut for in-depth research. “If you’re working on a dossier that you don’t know so much about and you let AI help you come up with questions to ask in parliament, that’s a problem.”
“Faster and smarter”
MP Daniël van den Berg, of the right-wing opposition party JA21, said: “I think it would be a shame for me to spend hours trawling through minutes and documents looking for media items. AI helps me do it faster and smarter.”
But Marleen Stikker, founder of De Digitale Stad, one of the Netherlands’ first online networks, said using AI in parliament undermined Dutch democracy.
“We are outsourcing our democratic system to the American AI companies’ algorithms, which aren’t even neutral, they’re skewed. That’s absurd, surely?”

items.title: Children in Dutch care system exploited on placements abroad
items.summary: Children in the Dutch care system may be being exploited while on youth placements abroad, an investigation by current affairs...
items.body_text:
Children in Dutch care system exploited on placements abroad
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Children in the Dutch care system may be being exploited while on youth placements abroad, an investigation by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur has found.
Councils and child protection agencies can sometimes send children with behavioural problems to other countries, such as Spain, when there is no suitable place for them in the Netherlands. This is supposed to be a temporary solution but some end up staying for up to three years.
The investigation found that the health and youth care inspectorate (IGJ) has been flagging risks in the system since 2009, but parliament was never informed. The inspectorate now says it is receiving reports of children being forced into unpaid work, locked up and not going to school, and admits that nothing has changed.
Because the IGJ has no jurisdiction in foreign countries it cannot investigate reports itself. Some children are also being sent outside the EU, the investigation found, some to Morocco.
Those placed in Morocco have no background in the country, which the organisation running the site, Multi Plus Zorg, said is an advantage because it makes the children more dependent on staff and lets them focus on their own development. Youth law professor Mariëlle Bruning told the programme it “smells of abuse”.
The IGJ said “peer pressure” was being used in some places to keep children under control, and that some were subjected to “outdated” methods focused on punishment.
It also said it has reports of children being physically restrained and barred from leaving the grounds, neither of which is permitted in this type of care, and of some having to do heavy work instead of going to school.
The inspectorate last counted how many Dutch children were in care abroad in 2007, when there were 330.
Youth care minister Mirjam Sterk said she found the situation “worrying”. Parliament passed a motion earlier this year to limit placements abroad as far as possible.

Croatian couple on run from Slovenia arrested near Dutch border
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A Croatian couple who went into hiding in the Netherlands after being sought in connection with a murder in Slovenia have been arrested across the border in Germany.
The 31-year-old man and 29-year-old woman were stopped in Isterberg, near the border town of Nordhorn, by plainclothes police officers on Friday evening.
Police believe they had just crossed the border from the Netherlands because strict checks are in place on the German side.
Slovenian prosecutors had issued a European arrest warrant for the couple, who are suspected of torture, strangulation and murder.
German police took them into custody in Oldenburg, where they appeared in court on Saturday for an extradition hearing. Their car was also confiscated.
The Telegraaf reported that the couple had been living in the Netherlands and driving in a car with false registration plates. The man did not have a valid driving licence.

items.title: “Don’t be a creep”: Polish ice cream company launches campaign against sexual harassment of staff
items.summary: Good Lood has empowered its staff to refuse service to customers making inappropriate remarks.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Polish ice cream chain has launched a campaign to stamp out sexual harassment of staff by customers, including empowering employees to refuse to serve such clients.
The campaign is based around the fact that the Polish word for ice cream, “lody”, also has an informal vulgar meaning, referring to oral sex. The company, Good Lood, which runs 37 outlets, says that its female staff regularly suffer lewd comments from male customers incorporating this double entendre.
In response, in late August it launched a campaign titled “Nie bądź oblechem”, meaning “Don’t be a creep”, with information displayed prominently at its ice cream stands and on its social media platforms.
The firm said it condemned “crude remarks, inappropriate jokes and verbal harassment directed at service workers” and promised to support its staff in dealing with them. “Everyone deserves respect, without exception!”
Good Lood advised employees to respond to inappropriate comments with a short, firm retort such as “Great, that’s the 20th time I’ve heard that” or “Perhaps you could repeat that more loudly, so the rest of the queue can hear?” It also called on other customers to react if they witnessed such behaviour.
In a follow-up social media post last week, the company confirmed that staff had its backing if they decided not to serve a customer. “If someone is a creep and makes inappropriate comments and verbally harasses them, our team have the right to refuse them service.”
That post alone has so far garnered more than 50,000 likes or other positive responses on Facebook. Good Lood says that its messages posted as part of the campaign have already received over 10 million organic views on social media.
Comments on the company’s posts show overwhelming support, with many commenters sharing their own experiences.
“At last someone has spoken out about this!” wrote one, who said she worked in an ice cream parlour as a teenager.
“I remember how outraged I felt when I heard comments like that from men who could have been my fathers, or even my grandfathers. I wonder what would happen if someone spoke to their daughters or granddaughters like that.”
Good Lood says it want to start a broader conversation on what the “global issue” of harassment and disrespect towards front-line staff in retail and hospitality.
“Working in service or hospitality does not mean consenting to disrespect. The safety and wellbeing of our team will always come before profit. We are not afraid to lose a customer who cannot show basic human respect,” the company said in a press release.
Founded 10 years ago in Kraków, Good Lood now has 37 outlets there as well as in the Warsaw area. It also sells its products throughout Poland at Biedronka, the country’s largest supermarket chain.

items.summary: Poland has faced growing threats from Russia, including acts of sabotage and the entry of missiles and drones into its airspace.

Poland’s interior ministry has launched a TV campaign, including spots on public broadcaster TVP’s flagship morning show, aimed at educating the public about how to respond to emergency situations such as natural disasters and security threats.
The initiative comes as Poland has faced growing threats from Russia, including acts of sabotage and the entry of missiles and drones into Polish airspace. Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned this week that there may be an “escalation” of such actions in the coming weeks and months.

The new campaign will include weekend segments on the TVP1 channel and a series of pieces aired during TVP2’s breakfast show, Pytanie na śniadanie, which had an average audience of 322,000 in August, according to Nielsen Media data.
The weekend programmes will introduce topics such as floods, fires, extreme weather, power outages, chemical contamination, evacuation, cybersecurity, disinformation and first aid. Specialists will then discuss the subjects in greater detail during the morning segments.
The ministry says the content is based on its official security handbook, which it sent to all 17 million Polish households earlier this year, and is intended to help people prepare for emergencies before they occur.
“We only find out whether we’re prepared for difficult situations when they actually arise,” said Mateusz Jarecki, who is presenting the segments. “That’s why, in collaboration with specialists, we’ve produced a series of short, easy-to-follow videos that will help you prepare for various life scenarios.”
The government is sending copies of a booklet advising how to prepare for and act in emergencies to all 17 million households in Poland.
The guide includes information on what to do in the event of military attacks, terrorist threats and natural disasters https://t.co/xIaRQ2ie5N

According to Presserwis, a newsletter by media industry magazine Press, the ministry will spend 5.4 million zloty (€1.3 million) on broadcasting the campaign during Pytanie na śniadanie.
The agreement with the public broadcaster, signed on 4 September, includes 16 short segments and seven commentary pieces, according to Presserwis.
Pytanie na śniadanie’s website so far shows two segments with material from the series. One explains what to do when an evacuation order is issued, while the other covers what should be included in an emergency kit.
The campaign comes following recent criticism from the opposition over how the government communicates with citizens during emergencies.
Amid Russian mass attacks on western Ukraine this week, including strikes on a train and a truck near the Polish border, residents of eastern Poland received mobile phone alerts from the Government Security Centre (RCB) warning of air strikes and urging them to seek shelter.
However, Beata Mazurek, a senior figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, criticised the messages for “spreading panic without providing instructions” on where people should shelter.
“Where are we supposed to go? That seems to be the most basic piece of information. The threat is real, but the instructions are incomplete,” she wrote on X.

items.title: Moose on the loose at Warsaw’s main station brings trains to a standstill
items.summary: Disruptions lasted over 80 minutes before the animal was tranquilised and sent back to the forest.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A moose wandered onto the tracks at Warsaw Central Station on Sunday evening, disrupting rail services in the Polish capital for more than 80 minutes before it was safely removed.
The animal first appeared on a platform before moving onto the tracks, forcing Polish Railway Lines (PLK), the company responsible for Poland’s rail infrastructure, to suspend, cancel and divert several train services.
View this post on Instagram
Videos and photographs shared online showed the moose lying on the tracks and running along the railway line at Warsaw Central, the capital’s busiest station, which is mainly underground and therefore not easy for such a large animal to access.
Police do not know how the moose ended up at the station, reports broadcaster TVN24. Officers were first alerted at 7:10 pm on Sunday and cordoned off the platform where the animal was located.
When emergency services arrived, the moose was tranquilised. It was then placed on a large sheet and carried out of the station by police officers and emergency workers before being loaded onto a specialist vehicle to be returned to a forested area.
PLK, which named the moose Emil, later confirmed that the animal had been safely removed and that normal train services were being restored.
The company added that the disruptions lasted just over 80 minutes, using a pun combining the Polish words for moose (łoś) and 80 (osiemdziesiąt) to produce the word “łosiemdziesiąt”.

— PLK SA (@PKP_PLK_SA) September 13, 2026
The Eurasian moose (also known as the Eurasian elk) has long been native to Poland, but by the mid-20th century hunting and habitat loss had brought the species close to extinction in the country.
Its population subsequently recovered, reaching an estimated 6,000 animals by the 1980s and around 30,000 by 2019, helped by a moratorium on moose hunting introduced in 2001.
Several hundred live in the Kampinos national park on the northwestern outskirts of Warsaw. They are therefore relatively frequent visitors to the capital, according to the Interia news website, although venturing onto train lines in the centre is unusual.
The growth in the moose population, combined with urban expansion and changes to its habitat, has led to other high-profile encounters in areas inhabited by humans. In 2022, a moose was spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in the northern Polish city of Elbląg.

items.title: Two longtime tenants parting ways with Tartu's legendary Genialistide Klubi
items.summary: Tartu's Genialistide Klubi is facing a shake-up as longtime subtenants Must Kast theater and Möku Bar plan to move out, citing the venue's uncertain future and desire to grow.
items.body_text:
Two longtime tenants parting ways with Tartu's legendary Genialistide Klubi
Tartu's Genialistide Klubi is facing a shake-up as longtime subtenants Must Kast theater and Möku Bar plan to move out, citing the venue's uncertain future and desire to grow.
Must Kast and Möku have both been mainstays at the self-described "subcultural" center for more than a decade, but say that uncertainty about Genialistide Klubi's future, along with plans to grow, prompted their respective decisions to move.
Genialistide Klubi, which has been located at Magasini 5 since 2008, has faced noise complaints from neighbors for nearly a year and a half. Although it has taken steps to reduce the noise, they have not yet been sufficient for the City of Tartu to release nearly €45,000 in program funding, leaving the club without that annual municipal support this year.
Must Kast is moving across town to the Estonian National Museum (ERM), with its first performances at its new home scheduled for early October. Director Merilyn Elge said the theater's needs have changed considerably over the years, particularly in terms of technical capacity and stability.
"We feel that Genialistide Klubi can no longer meet those needs," Elge said. "Over the past year, there have been so many questions hanging over the place, and no one has been able to answer them."
Möku, which first announced its plans to move late last week, plans to reopen at the Sisevete Saatkond, a historic river barge docked on the Emajõgi at Vabaduse puiestee 5, by mid-December.
"We like running a boring bar where people can come for no reason," co-owner Kaarel Jõudvald said. "Genialistide Klubi is a cultural and events venue."
He added that the move, the bar's second since relocating to the club from Rüütli tänav in 2015, will also give Genialistide Klubi a chance to try running its own bar.
'We're looking for meaningful partners'
Möku's revenue has covered a large share of Genialistide Klubi's rent. Even so, manager Juhan Kari said the club expects to find new operators and continue serving as a platform for emerging cultural projects.
"A subcultural center is by nature constantly changing, and Genklubi has been a creative incubator all these years," Kari said. "We're not merely looking for tenants to fill the space or sell beer; we're looking for partners who bring something meaningful to the table."
Several interested parties have already reached out to the club, he added, but it's still too soon to provide any details.
Genialistide Klubi also still expects to secure this year's earmarked municipal funding after making some changes to its program. August noise measurements fell within permitted limits, putting the city in a position to release the funding.
"The exact amount will depend on the application Genialistide Klubi submits, how many events have taken place and how many are planned," said Tartu Department of Culture director Sten Svetljakov.
The city, he added, will meet with the club Wednesday to discuss further.
Founded in 2006 by members of the eponymous Estonian band Genialistid, Genialistide Klubi first opened its doors at the former Lutsu Theater House nearby, which now houses Tartu Toy Museum's Theater House.
The club relocated to its present home on Magasini tänav two years later.
--
Editor: Marko Tooming, Aili Vahtla

items.title: Datasel seeks resolution in Estonia ammunition dispute
items.summary: India‑owned Datasel says it is ready to resolve a dispute over ammunition deliveries and meet Estonia's quality and quantity requirements, according to a proposal sent to the government and the Ministry of Defense.
items.body_text:
Datasel seeks resolution in Estonia ammunition dispute
India‑owned Datasel says it is ready to resolve a dispute over ammunition deliveries and meet Estonia's quality and quantity requirements, according to a proposal sent to the government and the Ministry of Defense.
The Italian company with Indian owners, Datasel, sent a proposal to the government, the Ministry of Defense and the Center for Defense Investment (RKIK), stating that it wishes to resolve the situation constructively and is prepared to deliver all ammunition specified in the contract. The letter was addressed to all ministers, including Prime Minister Kristen Michal, RKIK director Elmar Vaher, two other officials, and 17 members of parliament.
In the letter, the company outlines steps for reaching a solution.
"Datasel's position is clear: we remain willing and prepared to complete the contractual supply. Our objective is not to prolong the present dispute, but to establish a practical framework that protects the interests of Estonia, objectively addresses the outstanding technical and contractual matters, and enables the underlying defence procurement requirement to be fulfilled," the letter states.
The company added that it has already taken significant financial commitments and organized supply chains to fulfill the contract. "Significant resources have been committed towards raw materials, components, manufacturing and associated procurement activities necessary for completion of the supply," Datasel noted.
According to Datasel, it is able to fulfill its contractual obligations immediately once the financing framework is set. The company is willing to agree on a schedule with Estonian authorities and ensure transparency in production, inspection and delivery.
Estonian authorities have said that the ammunition delivered so far by Datasel was of poor quality. Datasel says it is ready to ensure that the ammunition meets Estonia's required standards.
"Datasel's objective is not simply to complete the outstanding quantities, but to complete them through a controlled and verifiable process capable of providing Estonia with confidence in the material ultimately delivered," the company stated.
Datasel says it is willing to cooperate with the relevant Estonian agencies to ensure quality control, inspection and testing according to specific requirements before further deliveries are made.
In the letter, Datasel proposes that representatives of the Estonian government and RKIK begin dialogue immediately to reach an agreement. First, a decision must be made regarding the ammunition already delivered, and it should receive an independent technical assessment. What happens with the remaining deliveries must be agreed together, including how inspection, testing, acceptance and documentation will be carried out.
Datasel also wants both sides to work toward resolving contractual and legal disagreements. For this, the company proposes forming a joint working group to handle technical, contractual, financial and logistical details and prepare a roadmap and timeline for moving forward.
The letter also notes that although Datasel does not withdraw its positions in the ongoing legal dispute, these disagreements should not prevent both sides from seeking a mutually acceptable solution through dialogue. "Datasel therefore respectfully expresses its readiness to engage directly with the appropriate representatives of the Government of Estonia and RKIK," the letter states.
Background
In 2024, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) signed four procurement contracts with Datasel S.R.L., an Italian company acquired earlier that year by Indian-owned Neco Defence Munitions. Despite neither Datasel nor its parent firm having any prior track record of manufacturing or selling artillery shells, RKIK wired roughly €70 million in advance payments.

items.title: Expert says Putin unlikely to ever seek peace deal with Ukraine
items.summary: Russia is attacking Ukraine with increasing force, and since Russian leader Vladimir Putin assumes that Russia can endure longer, it is not particularly likely that he will ever seek to conclude a peace agreement with Ukraine, says Kristi Raik, director of the International Center for Defense and Security (ICDS).
items.body_text:
Expert says Putin unlikely to ever seek peace deal with Ukraine
Russia is attacking Ukraine with increasing force, and since Russian leader Vladimir Putin assumes that Russia can endure longer, it is not particularly likely that he will ever seek to conclude a peace agreement with Ukraine, says Kristi Raik, director of the International Center for Defense and Security (ICDS).
Russia is trying to create fear not only in Ukraine but also among Ukraine's allies, attempting to weaken Europe's willingness to continue supporting Ukraine, Raik noted.
"And it constantly looks for new means to do so, because things are not going well for Russia in the war right now. That is why they have begun taking more risks, escalating in the hope that Europe is not ready to adopt stronger countermeasures. And in that sense, unfortunately, they are right — the countermeasures by European states have so far been quite weak," she said.
It cannot be said that Western countries have taken no countermeasures at all, but these remain weaker than expected, Raik added, pointing for example to Germany's reaction to the incident at Leipzig‑Halle Airport.
"It is very important that support for Ukraine continues, that there is no sign Russia can achieve through its attacks that we would somehow become afraid of supporting Ukraine. On the contrary, this is precisely the critical moment when everything must be done to help strengthen Ukraine's air defense and tighten sanctions against Russia — and there are still many options that have not yet been dared to use," she said.
At the Arctic meeting in Rovaniemi, Friedrich Merz and Donald Tusk warned of decisive moments in the coming weeks. According to Raik, the warning referred to Russia planning further attacks in Europe.
"Understandably, the countries whose support is most important for Ukraine — led by Germany — are the main targets. In Western Europe, people tend to think the Baltic states are the primary target, but recently that has not been the case, and I think the ground for Russian influence operations is unfortunately more favorable in Germany or France than in the Baltic states," Raik said.
At the same time, U.S. President Donald Trump has not done anything significant to pressure Russia, although at times his attitude toward Ukraine has become more positive, she noted.
Asked whether the main problem in U.S.‑mediated talks is that Washington wants peace much more than Moscow — and that Moscow does not actually want peace at all — Raik replied that at present this can indeed be said.
"Having been to Ukraine myself, I can say that no one in Ukraine believes the war will end before next spring. On the contrary, Russia is attacking more forcefully, and Putin's assumption remains that they can endure longer. And I do not consider it likely at all that Putin personally would ever seek to conclude any peace agreement with Ukraine," Raik said.
"He still cannot achieve the goals he has set for himself in Ukraine. So from his perspective, the only alternative is to continue the war — perhaps at best to limit military activity at some point if it becomes too costly and too dangerous for Russia," she added.
The ICDS is the leading think-tank in Estonia specialising in security, defense and foreign policy issues.
--
Editor: Marko Tooming, Argo Ideon

items.title: Kosovo’s New Govt Challenged in Court as Presidential Pick Withdraws
items.summary: Political crisis worsens as opposition PDK contests legality of Albin Kurti's re-election as Prime Minister, and Bekim Sejdiu withdraws his bid to become President.
items.body_text:
Kosovo’s New Govt Challenged in Court as Presidential Pick Withdraws
Prime Minister Albin Kurti’s cabinet take their seats in parliament, September 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN.
The opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, on Tuesday asked the country’s Constitutional Court to assess whether the parliamentary vote that re-elected Albin Kurti as Kosovo’s Prime Minister three days ago was valid.
“We consider that parliament has been inaugurated by violating the constitution. A parliament which is inaugurated unconstitutionally cannot produce constitutional institutions,” Perparim Gruda, a PDK MP, told media on Tuesday.
“Even earlier, we called [on parliament] to not proceed with further decisions before clarifying question marks,” Gruda added.
Tuesday’s filing by the PDK is the second in as many days that it has taken to the top court. On Monday, it complained to the court that Sunday’s inauguration of parliament had violated the rules.
The PDK claims that Kurti’s ruling Vetevendosje party violated the 30-day deadline to inaugurate parliament and that the assembly cannot be considered inaugurated until all five deputy speakers are elected.
On Sunday, the PDK withdrew its candidate for the post of deputy speaker, while four other deputies were elected.
Vetevendosje leader Kurti was re-elected Prime Minister by MPs at a session boycotted by opposition parties. A narrow majority of 62 MPs out of 120 voted in favour of Kurti’s new cabinet. Eight MPs from the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista voted against.
However, on Monday evening, the election of a new state President received another setback when the sole candidate for the post, Bekim Sejdiu, announced his withdrawal following disagreements within his Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, over his candidacy.
Kurti and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku had agreed on his name on August 31 – but six LDK MPs then announced they would not support him, leaving the potential vote without the necessary quorum.
Failure to elect a new President within two months of the inauguration of parliament would trigger new elections, the fourth within less than two months.
“Under such circumstances, characterised by the lack of the necessary parliamentary support for my election as President and by the deviation of the entire process into the vortex of internal political dynamics and clashes, I have decided to withdraw from the candidacy for President,” Sejdiu, a former Constitutional Court judge and diplomat, said in a Facebook post.
“I call on the political parties to find a way out of this vicious circle, which, more than anything else, is eroding citizens’ hopes of a prosperous future for them and their families,” he added.
LDK leader Abdixhiku lamented the lack of support for his candidacy. “His withdrawal in the face of political hysteria shows exactly why a person with such a character would be an appropriate pick for President,” Abdixhiku said.
“It’s a pity that we don’t have a President today. Instead of a solution, we have political chaos, a blockade as a means, and new elections, once again, as a goal,” he added.
Vetevendosje also regretted the withdrawal – and accused opposition MPs of trying to provoke new elections.
“When a boycott is used to make a vote impossible, then we don’t have political difference around a candidate but the blockage of a constitutional process and taking the country to repeated elections,” Vetevendosje said.

items.title: Serbian Students Stage ‘Victors’ March’ to Register for Polls
items.summary: Thousands of supporters joined the student movement as it officially filed its registration with the electoral commission for the October elections on Monday evening.
items.body_text:
Thousands of supporters of Serbia’s opposition Student List gathered on Monday evening in front of the University of Belgrade Rectorate and marched to the Republic Electoral Commission to register their candidate list, “Student List – Students Win”, for the snap parliamentary elections on October 25.
Participants in what the Student List called the “Victors’ March” brought with them a replica of the Victory monument, a prominent Belgrade landmark and symbol of the city.
At the weekend, people queued in cities and towns around Serbia to sign their names in support of the Student List, sometimes waiting in line for a couple of hours.
Student List arose from the long-running student-led protest movement that was established after the Novi Sad railway station disaster in November 2024. It is seen as the main opposition challenger to the long rule of the Serbian Progressive Party of President Aleksandar Vucic.
Vucic plans resign as head of state and campaign for the prime minister’s post in the election. “On September 27 I will resign as president. That evening, I will address the nation and thank people for their support,” Vucic told Pink TV on Sunday.

items.title: Truth and Consequences: Kosovo Special Court to Deliver High-Stakes Verdict
items.summary: As the Kosovo Specialist Chambers prepares to deliver its verdict in the case of Hashim Thaci and his co-accused, the stakes could hardly be higher – for the defendants, the court, Kosovo, and transitional justice itself.
items.body_text:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip
On September 16, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague will pronounce its long-awaited verdict in the case against Hashim Thaci, former president of Kosovo, and three other former commanders of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA – Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi.
Each was charged by the Specialist Prosecutor’s Office with multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, allegedly occurring in 1998-2000 during and shortly after the brutal war with Serbian forces.
The case, followed widely, is currently the world’s only “senior leadership” war crimes trial. The verdict, whatever it might be, will have profound consequences for numerous stakeholders: the accused, Kosovo at large, the victims, the prosecution, and the court itself; and also for the European Union and its related organisations, given the extraordinary amount of time and resources invested: 18 years [2008-2026] and a jaw-dropping 500 million euros.
Of course, factors such as time and money should not influence the court’s decisions. But Edward Joseph, an attorney and professor at Johns Hopkins University, and an expert on Kosovo and the Balkans, raised thought-provoking questions in an article in Kosovo Online on July 5, 2026, worth quoting in its entirety:
“Like everyone else, I am simply observing. I would say that I am concerned. I will not make predictions, but I am concerned that there could be, consciously or unconsciously, a motivation for this court to convict the defendants,” Joseph wrote.
“Otherwise, how would they justify this years-long and extremely expensive process, their high salaries, their staff, and all of the institutional support? They have a substantial budget, and then you take former President Hashim Thaci, remove him from office, bring him there, and in the end you have nothing? Not a single conviction? That is why I am concerned that this could become a conscious or unconscious motivation.”
To properly understand the enormity of the investment, and to consider answers to these questions, it is important to recall the benchmarks of time and money over the years.
The investment of time
Supporters of the former KLA leaders hold images of Hashim Thaci and Kadri Veseli during a rally in Pristina, February 2026. Photo: EPA/Georgi Licovski.
The seed for the Specialist Chambers and Specialist Prosecutor’s Office was planted in 2008.
Carla Del Ponte, former chief prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, ICTY, wrote in her memoir, Madame Prosecutor, of heinous crimes committed by members of the KLA against Serbs, minority Kosovars, and Albanian collaborators, including rampant human organ-trafficking.
Her stunning claims spawned a two-year investigation from 2008-2010 by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, PACE, headed by Swiss senator Dick Marty, resulting in a report titled ‘Inhuman treatment of people and illicit trafficking in human organs in Kosovo’.
The Marty Report corroborated many of Del Ponte’s accusations, and named some of the alleged perpetrators, including Hashim Thaci and Kadri Veseli, who were among the founders of the KLA.
The alleged crimes included murder, abductions, torture, forced disappearances, and involvement in organised crime; there was also mention of a “handful” of organ trafficking cases, far fewer than claimed by Del Ponte. The alleged victims, again, included Serbs, members of ethnic minority groups and political enemies of the KLA.
Though it lacked evidence, the Marty Report was adopted in its entirety by a resolution of PACE in January 2011, which mentioned organ trafficking eight times in its three pages.
PACE urged the EU’s rule-of-law mission in Kosovo, EULEX, to ensure the perpetrators were held to account. EULEX then authorised an extensive criminal investigation by the EU’s Special Investigative Task Force, SIFT, headed by Clint Williamson, the former US ambassador-at-large for wa

items.body_text:
Hungary ranks first among men’s teams and second among women’s teams in the latest water polo rankings released by European Aquatics.
The standings are based on the performance of senior and youth national teams over the past three years. Among the men’s teams, Hungary tops the list having finished in the top six in all of the last eight tournaments included in the ranking.
Szilárd Jansik (L) and Serbia’s Djordje Lazic in the final of the Men’s Water Polo European Championship in Belgrade n January 25, 2026. Photo: MTI/Czeglédi Zsolt
The team secured silver medals at the senior European Championship in Belgrade and the U16 European Championship in Istanbul.
Serbia, the current European champions, hold second place, while Spain takes third.
The silver medalist Hungarian team at the awards ceremony for the Men’s Water Polo European Championship in Belgrade on January 25, 2026. Photo: MTI/Czeglédi Zsolt
In the women’s category, only the European champions from the Netherlands rank ahead of Hungary.
The Dutch team successfully defended their title, winning again in Funchal this year, just as they did in Eindhoven two years ago. Spain finishes in third place.
The Hungarian team at the Women’s European Water Polo Championship in Funchal on February 5, 2026, before the Hungary-Netherlands match. Photo: MTI/Szigetváry Zsolt
The federation also published an overall combined ranking, which is led by Hungary, ahead of Spain and Greece.

items.title: Three Men Sentenced in Catania Sexual Assault Case Involving Hungarian Tourists
items.summary: The Criminal Court of Catania sentenced two Moroccan men to 7 years and 2 months in prison each for the sexual assault of two Hungarian female tourists in Sicily last year, and their third accomplice to 7 years and 4 months—the first-instance verdict was handed down on Monday. The men, aged 23 to 26, were […] The post Three Men Sentenced in Catania Sexual Assault Case Involving Hungarian Tourists appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
Italian prosecutor vows full justice as suspects face group sexual violence charges; case cracked thanks to victim’s quick-thinking sister and phone tracker.Continue reading
The Criminal Court of Catania sentenced two Moroccan men to 7 years and 2 months in prison each for the sexual assault of two Hungarian female tourists in Sicily last year, and their third accomplice to 7 years and 4 months—the first-instance verdict was handed down on Monday.
The men, aged 23 to 26, were convicted of sexual assault by multiple perpetrators, as well as drug possession and forcing the victims to use drugs. The case was tried under expedited proceedings, so one-third of the original potential sentence was waived. Marof Hamza and Arsab Marvan each received seven years and two months in prison, while Barsan Szufian received seven years and four months.
Since their arrest last year, the perpetrators have been held separately in different Italian prisons.
They were present when the verdict was read, but were not given the opportunity to speak after the court’s decision was announced.
At the time of the crime, all three Moroccan nationals were in Italy as illegal immigrants; however, they were not sentenced for this offense in this proceeding.
The court will issue a separate ruling on the compensation to be awarded to the women. The Italian state fund established for victims of violence will also contribute to the amount.
Massimiliano Scaringella, the attorney representing the two Hungarian women, told MTI that he is satisfied because “this is a significant ruling that reaffirmed that such things cannot happen in Italy. Such behavior cannot be tolerated and will not be accepted. The court found the accounts of the young women who suffered the assault to be entirely credible.”
The two women did not attend the hearings. Massimiliano Scaringella emphasized that the victims had experienced trauma and wished to remain absent to protect their privacy.
As Hungary Today reported, in the final days of August last year, the tourists accepted a ride back to their lodging from the two defendants on the beach in Catania; however, the defendants instead took them to a remote location, where their third accomplice joined them. They then forced the two women to use cocaine and subjected them to sexual acts against their will. The police managed to track down the group in the town of Paterno, thanks to the younger sister of one of the victims, who reported the two young women as missing and activated a phone tracking service that allowed her to locate their cell phones.
Earlier, Sebastiano Ardita, deputy prosecutor in Catania, told MTI that following the verdict, the Moroccan men must serve their prison sentences either in Italy or in their country of origin, provided that their country of origin guarantees they will serve the full sentence there. Sebastiano Ardita emphasized that Italian authorities, including prosecutors’ offices and courts, treat the punishment of sexual assault as a priority. He explained that the Italian Criminal Code does not distinguish between the terms “sexual assault” and “sexual aggression.”
Via MTI; Featured photo:Pexels (Illustration)

items.body_text:
The bonds are expected to be listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange in the coming months.Continue reading
The Hungarian oil and gas company MOL Plc. is preparing to issue a new euro-denominated bond. As the company announced on Monday on the Budapest Stock Exchange (BÉT) website, the planned issue size is up to €500 million.
The bonds will have a five-year maturity, carry a fixed interest rate, and be issued in registered form. The offering is part of the company’s €2 billion Euro Medium Term Note program, which was updated on September 10.
MOL has appointed a consortium of major international and regional banks to structure and execute the transaction. Participants include Citi, Erste Group, ING, and UniCredit, as well as Bank Pekao, OTP Bank, IMI-Intesa Sanpaolo, and Raiffeisen Bank International. Investor meetings began on Monday, September 14.
The announcement drew significant market interest.
MOL shares, listed in the premium segment of the BÉT, rose to a new record high of 5,460 forints (€14.87) shortly after the market opened on Monday. The shares then pared back some of their gains, trading at 5,390 forints (€14.68) at around 12:30 p.m.

items.title: He represented Hungary in the world championship final, but his citizenship was denied, citing national security
items.summary: Musza Arsunkaev is a talented 21-year-old wrestler who was born to refugee parents in Budapest. He only speaks Hungarian, but his request for citizenship was denied. Starting next year, he will no longer be able to compete without a Hungarian passport.
items.body_text:
He represented Hungary in the world championship final, but his citizenship was denied, citing national security
“I competed in the world championship final at age seventeen. When I was twenty, I represented Hungary in the final at the European championship, and now I’m fighting to get a Hungarian passport. Without a passport, I can’t achieve my dream of becoming a Hungarian Olympian and representing my country at the world’s biggest competition.”
— it was with these words that Musza Arsunkaev opened our conversation at the Vasas wrestling gym.
The athlete was born in Budapest in 2005, grew up in the Hungarian capital's 13th district and speaks perfect Hungarian. He attended school here from kindergarten through high school, graduating with his high school diploma just recently. He first stepped into the Vasas gym in 2014 alongside his brother, Ahmad; he played basketball before that, until his father noticed how skillfully and quickly he moved when he and his brother were wrestling in the living room.
Arsunkaev competes in freestyle wrestling and last year he became the Hungarian champion amongst the adults. He is proud of his first major success—reaching the U17 World Championship final—though he was a bit disappointed that he lost. In the semifinals, however, he pulled off a last-minute comeback against an Iranian competitor. He hopes that that particular match reflects his personality as an athlete and his mindset of never giving up, as well as his ability to pull off something unexpected in the final moments, which can have a decisive influence on the outcome.
He is currently preparing for this year’s U23 World Championships, which will be held in Las Vegas in October. He believes that winning the national qualifier in the 97-kilogram weight class will be easier than entering the United States due to the strict requirements. This is because he only has a non-biometric refugee passport, which must be renewed annually in Hungary, and airlines may even ask him not to board the flight in Budapest, as it’s not certain he’ll be allowed to continue his journey during a layover.
“My father, Abdulrasid, was born in Chechnya and grew up near Grozny; today he sells antique jewelry. My mother, Merci, was born in Nigeria and grew up near the capital, Lagos. My mom came to Europe in the early ’90s; her passport had expired, so she couldn’t return home with it and ended up in a refugee camp. She will soon earn her Hungarian high school diploma-she learnt Hungarian fluently, and only has a slight accent. She met my father in the camp; at first, it seemed like theirs would be nothing more than a passing fling, because they both envisioned their lives heading in different directions. Then, just like in a romantic movie, my mother told my father that my older brother was already on his way.”
They got married, and it turned out that they were meant for each other after all. Then, a few years later, I came along—there are six of us siblings in all, my youngest sister is eight. My older brother no longer lives with us, but otherwise we’re a large and close-knit family. When I was little, they asked me whether I wanted to be Russian or Nigerian, because according to Hungarian law I couldn’t be Hungarian, even though I was born here. My parents didn’t want me to be a Russian citizen, so the other option—Nigeria—ended up on the paperwork,” he said.
Arsunkaev only faced discrimination at school once because of his skin color, and he stood up for himself. He didn’t leave Hungary until he was 15, and even then it was only because he was talented at wrestling and had to travel to a competition. His explosiveness, speed, and agility became apparent very quickly, and he also had perseverance. In fact, there has only been one week in his career so far when he didn’t want to wrestle. items.title: A TV2 hozzájárulásával adta le a közmédia A tanú című filmet az adásszünet után
items.summary: A közmédia megbízott vezérigazgatója arról beszélt Magyar Péternek, hogy a film jogait Mészáros Lőrinc cégcsoportja vásárolta meg.
items.body_text:
A Mészáros Lőrinc érdekeltségéhez tartozó TV2 vásárolta meg korábban A tanú című film sugárzási jogait – derült ki a Duna Médiaszolgáltató Zrt. válaszából, amit a Telex megkeresésére adtak.
Hétfőn Horváth P. András, a közmédia megbízott vezérigazgatója arról beszélt Magyar Péter miniszterelnöknek, hogy a „bejövetelük napján szembesültek azzal”, hogy Mészáros Lőrinc cégcsoportja megvásárolta Bacsó Péter filmjének „kizárólagos forgalmazási jogait”, ezért amikor le akarták adni a filmet, kölcsön kellett azt kérniük.
Ennek okairól és pontos körülményeiről kérdéseket küldtünk a közmédiának, a válaszból pedig kiderült, hogy Horváth P. András a TV2-re gondolt, amikor azt mondta, Mészáros Lőrinc cégcsoportjánál van A tanú forgalmazási joga.
Mint írták, A tanú című film a nemzeti filmvagyon részét képezi, és a forgalmazási jogaival a Nemzeti Filmintézet (NFI) rendelkezik, a sugárzási jogok tőle vásárolhatóak meg. „Amikor a Duna Médiaszolgáltató Zrt. megbízott vezetése eldöntötte, hogy a filmet műsorra tűzi, a közmédia rendelkezett egy korábban megvásárolt, 5 sugárzásra érvényes sugárzási joggal, amelyből egyet még nem használt fel. A protokoll szerint jeleztük a Nemzeti Filmintézetnek, hogy élni kívánunk a még érvényes sugárzási jogunkkal. Az NFI ekkor tájékoztatott bennünket, hogy a filmre a TV2 évekre szóló sugárzási jogot vásárolt kereskedelmi áron, amely magasabb szintű rendelkezést biztosít számára a közmédia 5 alkalomra érvényes sugárzási jogánál.”
„Ezért történt meg, hogy a TV2-nek hozzá kellett járulnia ahhoz, hogy a közmédia sugározhasson egy, a nemzeti filmvagyon részét képező filmet. A TV2 megkeresésünkre hozzájárult ahhoz, hogy a közmédia a tervezett időpontban műsorra tűzze a filmet”
– válaszolták a Telex kérdésére.
Az M1 hírcsatorna adását még július 7-én, délután négy órakor szakították meg, ami után az a szöveg jelent meg rajta, hogy a közmédia nem hazudhat, és elnézést kérnek azért, hogy évekig mégis ezt tették. Az adás végül 19:56-kor A tanú levetítésével indult újra. Az adásszünet utáni első filmbe 653 ezren néztek bele.

items.title: Történelmi mélyponton van a Duna vízhozama Romániában, de felfüggesztették a kotrási munkálatokat, mert lejárt a szerződés
items.summary: Bár elméletileg vészhelyzeti készültségben van az ország, az atomreaktorok újraindítása egyre távolabbi tervnek tűnik, mert egyelőre aláírásokra várnak, hogy folytathassák a vízhozam növeléséhez szükséges intézkedéseket.
items.body_text:
Történelmi mélyponton van a Duna vízhozama Romániában, de felfüggesztették a kotrási munkálatokat, mert lejárt a szerződés
Történelmi mélyponton van a Duna vízszintje, de a bürokrácia miatt leálltak a munkálatok, amelyek hozzájárulhatnának a vízhozam növeléséhez, a vészhelyzeti készültség már csak nyomokban figyelhető meg, és a csernavodai atomerőmű újraindítása egyre távolabbi céllá válik.
Szeptemberben jelentősen csökkent a Duna vízszintje, az előző hónaphoz képest is alacsonyabbra süllyedt, a csernavodai atomerőmű számára szükséges vízhozam biztosításához nélkülözhetetlen kotrógépet azonban már nem használják. A kotrási szerződés augusztus 30-án lejárt, a kormány pedig nem hozott új határozatot a munkálatok folytatásáról.
Korábban még azt hangsúlyozták, már nem a blokkok újraindításáért küzdenek, hanem azért az alapvető vízmennyiségért, ami ahhoz kell, hogy a lekapcsolt reaktorok forró fűtőelemei ne hevüljenek túl. Szeptember másodikán jóváhagyták, hogy bárkákból, mobil gátakból és szivattyúkból álló védelmi rendszerrel tereljék a folyó megmaradt vizét a hűtőrendszerhez. Most azonban a legtöbb munkálat aláírásra váró papírok miatt szünetel.
2026. augusztus végén a Duna vízhozama az országba való belépéskor 1600 köbméter/másodpercre csökkent, ami két és félszer kevesebb az erre az időszakra jellemző, 3900 köbméter/másodperces átlagnál.
Csernavoda térségében három munkagéppel végeztek kotrási munkálatokat, illetve egy 150 méter hosszú kőgátat is építettek, hogy versenyt futva az idővel biztosítsák az atomerőmű reaktorainak hűtéséhez szükséges vízmennyiséget.
Két héttel később, szeptemberben a vízhozam drámaian, 1250 köbméter/másodpercre csökkent, a munkálatokat pedig ahelyett, hogy felgyorsították volna, jelentősen visszafogták.
Augusztus végéig az Alsó-Duna Vízügyi Igazgatósága (AFDJ) és az Országos Vízügyi Hatóság (ANAR) három munkagépet használt a Duna medrének módosítására Csernavoda térségében.
A három közül a leghatékonyabb, az AFDJ kotrógépe, amely naponta 7000-8000 köbméter üledéket képes eltávolítani. Ez a gép azonban nemrég elhagyta a munkaterületet, mivel a kotrási szerződés augusztus 30-án lejárt.
Jelenleg Giurgiu térségében állomásozik, mintegy 200 kilométerre Csernavodától.
Az Országos Vészhelyzeti Bizottság augusztus 21-i határozata előírta, hogy sürgősségi eljárásban minden rendelkezésre álló kotrógépet mozgósítani kell, de úgy tűnik, hiába. Bár az ANAR két másik, kevésbé hatékony munkagépet vezényelt át a térségbe az AFDJ kotrógépének pótlására, ezek együttes kapacitása annak alig a felét teszi ki.
A vízügyi hatóság augusztus 20-i műszaki jelentése szerint legalább 3–4 kilométeres szakaszon kellene kotrást végezni a Dunán, hogy Csernavoda irányába elegendő vízhozamot biztosítsanak.
Annak ellenére azonban, hogy a közlekedési minisztériumtól forrásokat kértek, továbbra sem született új kormányhatározat, amely lehetővé tenné a munkálatok folytatását más kritikus területeken, például Mărleanu és Rasova térségében.
Emellett a Csernavoda térségében épített kőgát sem bizonyult hatékonynak. A román sajtónak nyilatkozó szakértő szerint valójában sokkal hosszabbnak kellene lennie, ehhez azonban hatalmas beruházásra és a hajózás leállítására lenne szükség.
A szükséges erőforrások és idő hiányában a hatóságok katonai uszályok és pontonok használatát is mérlegelik, a vízszint azonban ehhez a beavatkozáshoz még nem elég alacsony.
A csernavodai atomerőmű blokkjai egyébként már a nyár közepén sorban elestek a Duna drasztikus apadása miatt: az 1-es reaktort július 28-án, a 2-est augusztus 13-án kapcsolták le, amikor a normál áramtermeléshez szükséges, óriási mennyiségű hűtővizet már nem tudták a turbinákhoz juttatni. Ezzel az ország villamosenergia-termelésének mintegy egyötöde – nagyjából 1400 megawatt kapacitás – tűnt el a hálózatból. Az energiaügyi minisztérium már augusztus végén elismerte, hogy az újraindításra egy jó ideig még semmi esély, a szeptemberre jelzett újabb apadás nyomán pedig már nem a termelés visszaállítás

items.body_text:
Prague Has the Most Unaffordable Rents for Minimum-Wage Earners in the EU
Prague Morning
Prague has the highest rent-to-minimum-wage ratio among EU capitals, with the average two-bedroom apartment costing 185% of the gross minimum wage.
Prague has become the European Union’s least affordable capital for minimum-wage earners looking to rent a home, according to a new analysis by the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC).
The average monthly rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the Czech capital reaches €1,710, compared with a gross monthly minimum wage of €924. This means rent alone amounts to 185% of the minimum wage.
Lisbon follows in second place, with rent accounting for 168% of the gross minimum wage. Budapest ranks third at 159%, followed by Bratislava at 158%.
Other capitals where average rent exceeds the gross minimum wage include Sofia (154%), Athens (153%), and Riga (151%).
The figures highlight the pressure facing minimum-wage earners in cities where housing costs have risen significantly faster than incomes.
How Prague Compares with Western Europe
Prague’s position is particularly striking when compared with several Western European capitals.
In Paris, average rent accounts for 138% of the gross minimum wage, while the figure stands at 125% in Madrid and 113% in Dublin.
At the other end of the ranking, Brussels is the most affordable capital for minimum-wage earners in the comparison. Average rent there represents 70% of the gross minimum wage. Berlin follows at 76%, while the figure is 85% in Nicosia and 87% in Luxembourg.
Housing Costs Across the EU
According to Eurostat’s latest figures cited in the analysis, housing and utility bills account for 23.6% of household spending across the European Union.
The ETUC has called for stronger collective bargaining, greater consideration of housing costs when setting minimum wages, and increased investment in social housing.
The organisation also noted that rents can be more affordable when measured against national minimum wages rather than those in capital cities. Among the 16 EU countries analysed, the share of the gross minimum wage required for rent ranged from 33% in Poland to 61% in Malta.

items.body_text:
Prague 8 Pirates to Host English-Language Guide to Czech Local Elections
Prague Morning
EU citizens living in Prague 8 can learn how to vote in the upcoming municipal elections at an event on 17 September.
The Prague 8 branch of the Czech Pirate Party is inviting international residents to an English-language evening explaining how EU citizens can take part in Czech local elections.
The event, titled “Hey, You Can Vote Too!”, will take place on Thursday, 17 September, at 6 PM at Pauza Palmovka in Prague 8.
The evening will offer a practical introduction to the Czech voting system, an overview of the Prague 8 Pirates’ local programme, and an opportunity for international residents to share their views on life in the district.
Organisers say the event is intended to help EU citizens understand their voting rights and discuss what they would like to see improved in Prague 8.
Who Can Vote in Czech Local Elections?
Citizens of other EU Member States can vote in Czech municipal elections if they meet certain conditions.
Voters must:
- Be at least 18 years old by the second day of the election.
- Have permanent or registered temporary residence in the municipality.
- Be entered in the supplement to the permanent electoral register.
EU citizens who are not already registered must apply by 7 October 2026 at 4 PM.
“Many people from other EU countries live in Prague 8, work here, raise their families here and use the same schools, parks, streets and public services as everyone else. Yet many still do not know that they can vote in local elections,” said Martin Štěrba, the Czech Pirate Party’s candidate for mayor of Prague 8.
“We want to explain how it works and hear directly from them what Prague 8 could do better.”
The Czech municipal elections will take place on 9 and 10 October 2026.
Voters in Prague 8 will elect representatives to both the Prague 8 Municipal District Council and the Prague City Assembly.

items.body_text:
Nearly 40 Percent of Young Czechs Experience Financial Stress Every Month
Prague Morning
Money worries affect almost one in three Czech adults, but younger people are facing a greater burden.
A new survey found that 39 percent of people aged 18 to 26 experience financial anxiety at least once a month, with household income playing a major role in how people feel about their finances.
Financial concerns are common across the Czech Republic. According to a survey conducted by Ipsos for Home Credit, 28 percent of adults experience worries about money at least once a month. Another 35 percent report financial stress several times a year.
Young adults face the greatest pressure
People aged 18 to 26 are the most likely to experience regular financial stress. Nearly four in ten respondents in this age group said they worry about money at least once a month.
Home Credit attributed the pressure partly to the cost of housing and everyday expenses. For young adults trying to establish themselves financially, rising prices in recent years have made it harder to absorb unexpected costs.
An unplanned bill or other expense can therefore create a serious problem, particularly for those who have limited savings.
Household income makes a significant difference
The survey found a clear relationship between household income and financial anxiety.
Among households earning up to CZK 40,000 per month, 41 percent of respondents reported experiencing financial stress. The proportion decreases as household income rises.
People living in households with monthly incomes above CZK 70,000 reported the lowest levels of financial concern.
Age and education also appear to influence how people view their finances. Respondents aged 54 to 65 and university students reported lower levels of stress than some other groups. In both categories, 43 percent said they did not experience financial stress at all.
Financial stress may also affect physical health
The consequences of financial difficulties can extend beyond anxiety and everyday worries.
The material also refers to research published by the American Mayo Clinic in 2025. According to the research cited, long-term financial distress and food insecurity may be associated with poorer cardiovascular health and a higher risk of death.
The findings underline the potential connection between financial security and overall well-being. However, the Czech survey does not establish whether financial stress directly causes health problems.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos in June 2026 among 1,026 people.

items.body_text:
PhotoEssay | Dimming Lights of Tbilisi’s Neighborhood Shops
Author: Gvantsa Lomaia.
*All photographs by the author
I only go to a small neighborhood grocery store – a “minimarket” – near my apartment block for two reasons: to buy cheap sausages for Rizha, the ginger stray dog we all have joint custody of, and whenever the supermarkets are closed.
Not that there are many options around. The ground floor of the newly built apartment block in Tbilisi’s Sanzona area where I live is occupied by commercial spaces, and many businesses have opened and closed there over the past decade: a gym, a mattress store, a used car parts shop, a delivery service, and a cafe that was a bit too cool for this place, but never one of those chain shops and supermarkets.
You have to walk blocks to reach them — the Nikora, the Libre, the Gvirila, the 2 Nabiji. Except for Europroduct – we haven’t quite made it to Europroduct territory yet.
So, before that particular kind of civilization reaches me with its loyalty cards, offers, discounts, and constantly rearranged shelves, I have to settle for a small non-chain mini marketi “Smile” nearby, where there is nothing to smile about, at least not at first glance.
The shop is always there, day and night, winter and summer.
Inside, everything is remarkably stable too: same products, same prices — if the prices ever change, it’s only upward. The bread is always in its place, so is the sausage, and so are the rock-hard Armenian gadas baked in someone’s home kitchen. There are no discounts, no special apps, and no notifications about offers. It doesn’t give me points, and neither does it ever remind me that I am a “valued customer.” It just stays open.
The only thing I see changing more or less regularly is the staff. I suspect the business does not offer high salaries.
And that’s why I keep wondering about the people who actually keep it going. Do they survive on regular customers? Do they still keep those old “nisia” notebooks where they record the products given out on credit? Does the staff have favourite customers?
What is it that still lures all those people in there?
“They’re just too lazy to stand in line elsewhere,” so the shopkeeper, the middle-aged Maya who works at my beloved corner shop, explains. “And also they love this shop,” she adds, somewhat surprised. She is sparing with her words, and I never get to ask her what it meant exactly to love your neighbourhood shop.
So I wander through different streets across the city, hoping at least other weary shopkeepers will tell me how, and why, a person might grow attached to their corner shops with the meagre selection of goods they offer.
That’s how I realise there are fewer such shops around than I imagined — the market giants have occupied all the strategic places. On those rare occasions I do find one, I’m not very welcome with my questions.
Perhaps the staff, often young people, simply don’t care – what kind of question is it anyways, whether they have a “favorite customer”… Or perhaps they think I am some kind of intrigani – a provocateur, someone trying to get them into trouble for one reason or another. You can’t trust anyone these days.
Or they are just tired – there is a visible sense of exhaustion on almost every face.
That’s one of the strange things about the fragile stability these shops offer: with no central corporate policies, you never know who and what awaits you there. Let it surprise you.
But at least Elza, a shop owner in Chugureti, is happy to talk, and, unlike most of the other shopkeepers I meet, she only warms up after learning I am a journalist. She asks me to remind the government that small business owners are struggling and would use some attention — I’ve already gathered as much myself.
Elza chats with me even if she, too, must be quite tired: she’s spent more than a decade in this shop. She’s the owner, assistant, accountant, and cleaner there. She and the shop barely manage to keep going, she says.

Georgian Dream MP Maia Bitadze Becomes New Culture Minister
Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has appointed ruling party MP and former Tbilisi Deputy Mayor Maia Bitadze as Minister of Culture, replacing Tinatin Rukhadze, who resigned in July.
Bitadze, who has served as a member of Parliament since 2020 and chaired the parliamentary committee on Environmental Protection and Natural Resources, will replace Rukhadze, who stepped down in July after less than two years in office, citing her health condition and the need for an “urgent course of treatment.”
Announcing the appointment, Kobakhidze highlighted Bitadze’s “exceptional, many years of management experience,” noting that she had previously served as Deputy Minister of Environmental Protection and Deputy Mayor of Tbilisi (2017-2020), including a period when she oversaw the culture sector. He also pointed to her academic background, noting that she holds a PhD in Law and is an Associate Professor at Tbilisi State University.
Kobakhidze said Bitadze was “distinguished by her conscientiousness,” describing it as the main “criterion” behind his decision to appoint her as a minister.
Bitadze described the appointment as “a great responsibility” and “an expression of trust” before the government team and those working in the cultural sector. “Culture is not only art and cultural heritage, but also part of our nation’s identity, our distinctiveness, and the language in which we must speak to the whole world,” she said, thanking her political team.
“I am coming into this field with many years of experience in public service, and also with a great desire to listen to every person who creates Georgian culture, who is a professional in the field, who cares deeply about it, and who loves this sphere,” Bitadze added.
First Deputy Culture Minister Mikheil Kiknadze had served as acting minister since Rukhadze’s departure.

- Academic background in journalism, social and political sciences, international relations, or another relevant field.
- Excellent written English, with the ability to write in a clear news style. Interest in and ability to write across a range of technical or creative genres will be considered an asset.

items.title: Georgian Dream now wants all major opposition parties banned
items.summary: The ruling party now intends to ban the only opposition group participating in parliament — For Georgia.
items.body_text:
Georgian Dream has announced plans to add the opposition For Georgia party to the list of parties it wants to ban. The list, which now contains five parties, covers all major opposition groups that managed to clear the electoral threshold in the 2024 parliamentary elections.
Georgian Dream intends to ban the five groups through a lawsuit at the Constitutional Court, which, if successful, would declare all of the groups unconstitutional.
For Georgia was founded by Giorgi Gakharia, who previously served as a Georgian Dream prime minister before moving to the opposition. They are the only opposition group who took up seats in parliament after the 2024 elections, ending their boycott in October 2025.
Irakli Kirtskhalia, Georgian Dream’s parliamentary leader, announced the decision on Monday, citing what he described as For Georgia’s ‘gross and brazen failure to recognise our country’s constitutional order, as well as numerous destructive actions by its members in parliament, in committees, and in their broader activities’.
Kirtskhalia did not specify which actions the ruling party considered ‘destructive’.
With Tuesday’s announcement, Georgian Dream is now seeking to ban all four major opposition parties that cleared the threshold in the disputed 2024 parliamentary elections, either independently or as part of coalitions with smaller partners. Its initial October 2025 lawsuit targeted Ahali, the United National Movement (UNM), and Lelo. In April 2026, the ruling party added the Federalists.
Initially, Georgian Dream excluded For Georgia from its list, citing its participation in parliament.
As the Constitutional Court normally has up to nine months to consider a case, and the deadline restarts when amendments are made to the lawsuit, some have speculated that Georgian Dream is seeking to prolong the process by adding new parties.
Kirtskhalia denied this on Monday, saying that if the ruling party wanted to ‘play’ with deadlines, it would have waited until ‘the final week’ to make additions to the lawsuit.
Gakharia’s party holds 12 seats in parliament, while Georgian Dream and its allies command 89. For Georgia also has a number of seats on municipal councils. Kirtskhalia said the lawsuit would not seek to revoke the parliamentary or municipal council mandates held by the party’s members.
Gakharia — who served as Georgian Dream’s Interior Minister from 2017 to 2019 and as Prime Minister until his resignation in 2021 — has been abroad since June 2025, a situation he has now openly described as ‘exile’. Criminal proceedings have been launched against him over episodes related to his time in government, and he faces a lengthy prison sentence if convicted.
Responding to the development via X on Tuesday, Gakharia said that by targeting For Georgia, Georgian Dream party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili is attempting to ban the country’s only ‘functional parliamentary opposition’.
‘Despite having the parliamentary majority, the Ivanishvili regime couldn’t stand even the single opposition party in the parliament, as they have nothing to respond to the critical voice’, he added.
Gakharia called plans to ban his party as ‘yet another step for the Ivanishvili regime to officially establish authoritarian rule in Georgia and suppress the political opposition’.
‘Banned or not, we will not back down from restoring Georgia’s democracy and safeguarding its European and Euro-Atlantic path’, he concluded.
‘Collective UNM’
Georgian Dream had promised its voters as early as the 2024 election campaign that it would ban what it calls the ‘collective UNM’ — a reference to the formerly ruling party and various other opposition parties that Georgian Dream claims act in concert with the UNM.
According to the ruling party, the UNM constituted a criminal regime during its 2003–2012 rule and has no legal right to exist. It has argued that other parties it claims are linked to the UNM should likewise not be allowed to function legally.

items.title: Azerbaijan detains atheist TikToker and man who attacked him, charges both with inciting religious hatred
items.summary: TikToker ‘Chevik,’ who has 90,000 followers, has gained public notoriety for criticising Islam online.
items.body_text:
Azerbaijan detains atheist TikToker and man who attacked him, charges both with inciting religious hatred
Azerbaijan’s State Security Service (DTX) has detained atheist TikToker Maksad Bagirov (Chevik) and a man who assaulted him for his religious beliefs. Both men were charged with inciting religious hatred.
Both Bagirov, the victim, and his assailant Kamran Bilalov were charged with inciting religious or ethnic hatred and enmity. Bilalov was also charged with a subarticle concerning the use of violence to incite hatred.
Bagirov, known as Chevik on TikTok, has around 90,000 followers on the platform. He is also a veteran of the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War. He has gained public attention for his videos in which he speaks out against Islam, figures regarded as sacred by Muslims, and Islamic religious teachings.
The men were detained on Monday.
According to the charges, Bilalov is accused of using violence against Bagirov because of his religious views, which he allegedly expressed publicly, including through videos shared in the media.
The investigation alleges that Bilalov intentionally used violence against Bagirov in a public place, causing him various bodily injuries, and committed acts aimed at inciting religious hatred.
Bagirov, who has nearly 90,000 followers on TikTok, was also arrested after the attack – on suspicion of inciting religious hatred by sharing videos containing statements that allegedly insult people’s religious beliefs and places of worship.
Bagirov is known for holding discussions and livestreams on TikTok focusing on religion and atheism. He has previously attracted the attention of law enforcement; in July he was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention under an article concerning acts that insult public morality, express clear disrespect towards society, and contain obscene language.
It is unclear which video or statements led to Bagirov’s prosecution.
In an unrelated case, on 2 September Bagirov was physically assaulted by two people in the city of Gabala, sustaining several injuries.
The investigation into case concerning Bilalov’s attack on Bagirov is ongoing.
Since late 2024, Azerbaijan has detained a number of TikTokers and social media influencers on a variety of charges, including insulting public moral values, hooliganism, threats, and the illegal collection of donations.
Some have described the mass arrests of TikTokers as part of the authorities’ crackdown on social media, while others have said the detentions reflect general growing restrictions on freedom of expression.

items.title: Review | Samanishvili’s Stepmother — a Georgian buddy comedy turned tragedy
items.summary: This newly remastered classic follows the merry adventures of middle-aged men as they seek a twice-widowed, childless older woman for a bride.
items.body_text:
3.5/5★
This newly remastered classic follows the merry adventures of middle-aged men as they seek a twice-widowed, childless older woman for a bride.
Based on Davit Kldiashvili’s 1897 novel of the same name, this Georgian classic is a mainstay of school curriculum and has repeatedly been adapted on-screen and to the stage. Yet the 1977 version — despite being directed by one of Georgia’s most famous filmmakers, Eldar Shengelaia (1933-2025) — has rarely been available for an English audience.
The film opens pretty much in the thick of the story, as the elderly Bekina Saminishvili (Vasil Kakhniashvili), the head of a noble yet impoverished, rural family, announces he wishes to remarry. His only son Platon (Imedo Kakhiani) does not take the news well, assuming that his father will immediately impregnate his new wife, have a son, and thereby force him to split his already meagre inheritance. As a solution to the brewing tension between father and son, they agree that Platon will become match-maker. His solution is to find a rare woman: one who has married twice but never given birth, under the assumption that such a woman would be infertile.
The majority of the film revolves around this search as Platon, accompanied by his perpetually cheerful (and perpetually drunk) brother-in-law Kirile (Nodar Chachanidze), roam far and wide in search of this elusive woman. The scenes are played as a bit of a buddy comedy, Kirile endlessly leading the two astray, as Platon wearily bears every new obstacle, which range from wedding brawls to mistaken identities at a funeral.
Eventually, Platon meets Aristo (Shota Gabelaia), another impoverished noble who claims his aunt Elene (Venera Neparidze) is such a woman. The two, along with Elene’s three step-sons via her second marriage, concoct a plan to ‘kidnap’ her, thereby avoiding shaming her former family for their inability to provide a dowry. Throughout this scheming, Elene herself is barely given a voice — ‘Nobody’s asking you. Let’s discuss’, her stepsons say, highlighting the lack of women’s agency within this traditional, hierarchical society.
Indeed, women are rare figures throughout the film, and when present, are often superseded by their male husbands, fathers, or brothers. While class consciousness is present throughout the film — the impoverished nobles still continue to assume a higher standing and attitude towards those they view as lessers including peasants and servants — women, no matter their status, are always simply expected to obey their male counterparts.
The last 20 minutes of the film are rushed as Bekina and Elene marry, only for her to become pregnant – the one thing Platon had dreaded from the start. By the film’s end, a son has been born, and the once-close family seems to have totally unraveled.
While many versions of the story put emphasis on the comedic aspects of the tale, Shengelaia instead more subtly depicts the tragicomedy of a rural Georgian noble class facing the rise of industrial capitalism, illustrating both their moral and physical failures. It is a depiction that surely did well with Soviet censors, yet still accurately translates Kldiashvili’s own conceptualisations, as well as standing tall on its own strengths.
The rushed ending, however, as well as being starkly dismal, could fail to connect with some viewers, who may wonder why so much emphasis was placed on the search for a bride rather than the existing family tensions.
The film’s audio, while cleaned up, also does not quite match with the original footage, which can be jarring at times. Certain lines go untranslated as well, which perhaps lessen the full extent of the humour.
Overall, however, Shengelaia’s adaptation is a faithful and beautifully shot portrayal of rural life in turn-of-the-century Georgia. It is well worth a watch, and in future, one can only hope it becomes more easily available to stream or purchase.

items.title: Police to get more powers to take down drones
items.summary: Unmanned devices like drones have taken on greater significance in today's security landscape, according to the interior ministry.
items.body_text:
The Finnish government has proposed expanding the police's powers to intervene with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) "to keep pace with technological developments", according to an interior ministry press release.
It said the proposal was submitted to parliament on Tuesday and that the legislation is set to go into effect "as soon as possible".
"Drones and other unmanned devices have become increasingly important in the current security environment. This development is not limited to aircraft; it also concerns unmanned vehicles operating on land, on the surface of the water and underwater," the ministry's release stated on Tuesday.
It noted that drone technology is widely used for legal and legitimate purposes, but noted the tech can also be used for criminal activities, including damaging critical infrastructure, disrupting authorities' work or invading privacy.
The use of force
"The current Police Act contains provisions on police powers to intercept the path of unmanned aircraft. According to the proposal, the police would in future have the right to intercept the movement and, more broadly, the operation of an unmanned vehicle regardless of whether it is operating in the air, on land, on the surface of the water or underwater," the release read.
According to the ministry, approved methods of UAV interception will include "technical devices, use of force and firearms".
"The proposal would also expand the Finnish Defence Forces' ability to provide executive assistance to the police in intercepting the movement or operation of an unmanned vehicle and other cooperation between authorities," the ministry explained.
