items.title: SA school charged after student hurt in hammer-throw incident
items.summary: SafeWork SA has lodged criminal proceedings against Christian Brothers College over a 2024 athletics incident in which a student was struck with a hammer-throw ball.
items.body_text:
SafeWork SA has lodged criminal proceedings against an Adelaide school over a hammer-throwing incident that seriously injured a student.
The safety watchdog alleges students and workers were "exposed to risks to their health and safety" when the incident occurred in September 2024.
What's next?
The matter is expected to appear in the SA Employment Court at a later date.
Criminal proceedings have been lodged against an Adelaide school after a student was seriously injured during an athletics training incident.
A Christian Brothers College student was struck in the head with a hammer-throw ball at St Albans Reserve at Clearview on September 5, 2024.
In a statement, SafeWork SA said a worker was also allegedly "exposed to the risk of being struck".
It said it had lodged the proceedings against Edmund Rice Education Australia Colleges Ltd, trading as Christian Brothers College (CBC), in South Australia's Employment Court earlier this month.
The safety watchdog said it had charged the school with a category two offence under the Work Health and Safety Act.
"It is alleged that workers and students participating in athletics training at St Albans Reserve, Clearview, were exposed to risks to their health and safety while undertaking javelin and hammer throw activities, in close proximity to each other, on 5 September 2024," SafeWork SA said in the statement.
"SafeWork SA alleges the school failed to provide adequate instruction or training to workers responsible for organising and supervising the athletics training and failed to ensure its safety policies and procedures were followed."
The safety watchdog said it would be further alleged that the school "failed to perform an adequate hazard identification and risk assessment for the athletics training".
According to the statement, the school allegedly "failed to maintain a safe work environment" by failing to ensure the hammer throwing was not carried out in close proximity to students participating in javelin and by not using a safety cage that complied with the relevant industry safety standards.
"SafeWork SA alleges these failures exposed workers and students to a risk of death or serious injury from being struck by a hammer throw ball," SafeWork SA said.
The matter is expected to appear in the SA Employment Court at a later date.
items.normalised_title: sa school charged after student hurt in hammer throw incident

items.title: Cowan warns BBL privatisation could 'spiral out of control'
items.summary: Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan believes the Big Bash League is already attracting the game's biggest star without private investment.
items.body_text:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan believes that the Big Bash League doesn't need to rush privatisation to compete with other T20 leagues around the world.
A Cricket NSW board member, Cowan told the ABC Cricket Podcast fears of a player exodus to rival leagues was premature, and a move toward privatisation could "spiral out of control".
Cricket Australia (CA) confirmed earlier this month that they would go ahead with an opt-in model that allows states to take their BBL teams to market with the option of selling stakes or entire franchises to private investors.
"[In previous seasons] they've been able to reshape scheduling, to reshape international stars and the salary cap around that. We've seen already there's no friction to attracting some of the world's best players," Cowan said.
"Ben Stokes is going to Adelaide, Finn Allen has just signed a mega deal. So the argument that is put forward is we're gonna lose players to the South African League. We haven't lost one yet.
"There's a view that the business could be run more effectively, which would enable some time to work out whether you actually do need to sell your star assets or not.
"Because when you start burning the furniture to warm the house, it can spiral quickly out of control from there."
The BBL has, in recent seasons, reshaped the fixture of the competition to make it shorter and in turn has increased viewership and attracted some of the games biggest names.
In the 2025/26 BBL season fans were treated to the likes of Colin Munro, Chris Jordan, Muhammed Rizwan and Sam Billings tearing up the competition. Coupled with Australian Test stars like Steve Smith, Alex Carey and Mitchell Starc who joined the tournament after their international duties finished.
Compare that with recent seasons of The Hundred where Mitchell Marsh, Adam Zampa, Jos Buttler and Trent Boult were some of the biggest name players in that competition, all of whom have played in the tournament or are set to play in the upcoming BBL16 season.
Cricket Australia believes that privatisation would allow the BBL to keep up with other T20 leagues around the world, like The Hundred in the UK and the SA20 in South Africa.
"There are opportunities now for our best Australian players to play in other leagues at the same time potentially with bigger salary caps. So when we talk about should we wait for two years or four years? No, we can't wait," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said.
"Those challenges are on our doorstep today. So we've got to make some decisions about how we compete.
"We're a relatively small country in a big global sport. So it's incumbent on us to make decisions that we can compete with elsewhere and that's exactly what we're doing."
Cricket NSW has been the most vocally opposed to the current model, while Queensland Cricket has also said it will likely have further questions but intends to hold on to its BBL franchise for the time being.
"We will closely monitor the sales process and at this stage, intend to retain 100 percent ownership of the Brisbane Heat, but of course remain open to private investment at the appropriate time," Qld Cricket Chair Kirsten Pike and CEO Terry Svenson said in a statement.
Meanwhile, Cricket Victoria is in support of the move, and will be the first to sell a license with the Melbourne Renegades set to be put to market to be sold in full.
"Private investment will unlock value for reinvestment across Victorian cricket, from the grassroots through to the elite game," Cricket Victoria Director Shaun Richardson said in a statement.
CA and the state's cricketing associations will continue negotiations ahead of the BBL16 and WBBL12 seasons starting, which are likely to be the last seasons involving the original eight franchises.

items.title: Failing to curry favour with the demographic
items.summary: It went straight to the Spamalot folder.
items.body_text:
Failing to curry favour with the demographic
When a 50-year-old actor said in Spectrum that, “I’ve got the knees and the back of a 90-year-old retired librarian”, it didn’t sit well with Nola Tucker of Kiama: “As an almost nonagenarian, retired librarian I take exception to Stephen Curry of The Castle fame comparing his knees and back to such as mine. What did he think we were doing? Tell him he’s dreaming.”
“Geoff Gilligan’s Greek translation tale (C8) gave me a laugh and reminded me of my sad attempt at learning German,” admits Peter Pocock of Hornsby. “The only thing I can remember is ‘the coat hanger is in the wardrobe’. Haven’t used it yet, but you never know.”
“When an AI (C8) breaks into a nuclear-armed country’s military system, hacks the launch codes and uses a few to see if they work, will the world be in an On the Beach situation?” asks Charles Haran of Noosa Heads (Qld). “If so, only a handful of oligarchs will be able to escape to Mars, and I suggest all the rest should band together NOW to stop it from ever happening.” We could always send them to Mars early.
“The article on self-driving cars brought to mind our recent experience in London,” writes Paul Koff of Glenhaven. “As we sped down the motorway, our Uber driver was extolling the virtues of his self-driving Tesla and its foolproof nature. To prove a point, he suddenly grabbed a guitar from the front passenger seat and began strumming it. We were taken aback and vaguely terrified, politely asking if he’d put his hands back on the wheel. He did so, laughingly telling us that many people have that reaction. Gee, how surprising.”
Rob Hosking of Paddington says he doesn’t think the Bee Gees (C8) “had reached the heights of their international fame when I passed Robin standing beside their battered Kombi in Park Street.”
Referring to “a celebrity encounter of the negative kind,” Charles Davies-Scourfield of Culburra Beach was “outside the Gazebo Hotel in the 1980s waiting for a cab with one other person. It was Christie Brinkley, the then wife of Billy Joel. A cab pulled up, and I heard her tell the driver she wanted to go into the city, as did I. ‘Would you mind sharing the cab please?’ said I. ‘Yes I would’ she said, closing the door.” Don’t worry Charles, she was probably only going uptown.
Column8@smh.com.au

items.title: One of Sydney’s largest councils joins ban on ‘pervert’ glasses at local swimming pools
items.summary: Councillors say locals have been raising concerns about people secretly filming in change rooms, swimming pools and around schoolsGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastOne of Sydney’s largest councils has joined the City of Brisbane and the City of Yarra to issue a ban on AI smart glasses at public pools as concerns mount over the potential for predators to exploit the new technology.On Tuesday evening, Canterbury-Bankstown voted overwhelmingly in favour of banning the tech
items.body_text:
One of Sydney’s largest councils has joined the City of Brisbane and the City of Yarra to issue a ban on AI smart glasses at public pools as concerns mount over the potential for predators to exploit the new technology.
On Tuesday evening, Canterbury-Bankstown voted overwhelmingly in favour of banning the tech at its pools, with its mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, describing them as “pervert glasses”.
Since their release, there have been reports of women being filmed without their consent and their interactions with a glasses-wearing influencer posted on social media.
“Chat groups, Facebook, local community forums and TikTok are just some of the online platforms where women are venting their concerns over the smart technology that threatens both safety and privacy,” El-Hayek told councillors at the meeting.
“Their biggest concerns are around ‘perverts and paedophiles’ secretly filming in change rooms, swimming pools and around schools.
“The latest AI smart glasses are wearable devices with high resolution cameras … and AI powered features like real time translation, object recognition and open-ear audio … these glasses can not only film, record and share footage, they can also scan your face and potentially access and retrieve information about you.”
Last month, Brisbane became the first council in Australia to publicly announce a ban on covert filming at its 21 public pools amid growing fears of threats to child safety.
The head of policy at Digital Rights Watch, Tom Sulston, praised the decision. He said it was “vital that councils across Australia ensure that public spaces like swimming pools are safe for families to enjoy without the threat of unwanted video surveillance”.
“We all need to be able to go out in public without fear of being covertly recorded and having the images uploaded to the internet without our consent,” he said. “We look forward to seeing not just councils following Brisbane’s lead, but also state and federal governments.”
Yarra in inner-Melbourne followed suit, voting last week to ban smart glasses from its leisure and aquatic facilities, childcare centres and playgrounds. It also confirmed it would call on the federal government to bring in stronger privacy laws to protect people from new technologies.
Randwick council in Sydney’s eastern suburbs has also banned the new technology at the Des Renford leisure centre. In a statement, it said “growing community concerns” about their potential misuse were behind the decision.
“Signage has been installed at the entrance and anyone wearing smart glasses in the centre will be asked to remove them or leave,” it said. “This precautionary measure will help ensure the centre remains a safe, welcoming and family-friendly place for all visitors.”
The bans will not apply to people with accessibility concerns, including vision impairment.
The federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, has not ruled out banning the glasses but has indicated how complex the laws are governing the new technology.
In August, she wrote to the privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, raising concerns she’d received from the community about their growing uptake and requesting it be given priority consideration.
“Privacy is an essential part of all our lives; it allows us to be who we are with dignity and without fear,” she said at the time.
“Unlike other forms of technology, smart glasses may be used more discreetly, making it harder to know when you are being recorded.
“The government is continuing to work on the next phase of privacy reforms to ensure our privacy laws are fit for purpose in the digital age.”
Australia’s online safety regulator has urged smart glasses companies to automatically blur people’s faces filmed on the devices, and make it clearer when someone is filming.

items.title: Australia’s Indigenous population estimated at 2.2m before ‘demographic catastrophe’ of colonisation
items.summary: Study finds earlier numbers were underestimated, suggesting impact of diseases and massacres were much greater than previously thoughtGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastThe number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia before colonisation was dramatically underestimated, according to new research that suggests many more of them were killed.Modelling by a national research group puts the population levels before the 1788 first fleet arrived at 2.2 mil
items.body_text:
The number of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia before colonisation was dramatically underestimated, according to new research that suggests many more of them were killed.
Modelling by a national research group puts the population levels before the 1788 first fleet arrived at 2.2 million, compared with early estimates of 250,000 people.
The research, by the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CIEHF), has been published in the peer-reviewed Nature Human Behaviour.
The authors wrote that, historically, population estimates have been poor “due to lethal diseases, frontier and structural violence, and absence of systematic censuses” and that it’s “invaluable to truth-telling and reconciliation” to try to rectify that.
They warn readers that the content of the study is confronting and possibly distressing.
The modelling showed there had to be millions of excess deaths from smallpox and other diseases, massacres, and the other results of colonisation such as dispossession and malnutrition, according to co-author Prof Corey Bradshaw, a global ecology professor at Flinders University.
His previous research found that an 1789 smallpox outbreak alone killed as many as 220,000 Aboriginal people. There were also other smallpox epidemics, as well as outbreaks of measles, influenza, tuberculosis, typhoid and other diseases.
Bradshaw said he would bet his career that massacre databases were underestimated by an “order of magnitude”.
“If you’re a frontier farmer, a colonialist that came out to a new area, and you were trying to remove people from ‘your’ land, you’re not going to write extensively about how many people you killed to do that,” he said.
“There’s another component here that’s essentially greed and racism – the entire concept of terra nullius was based on not many people being here. If there’s a systematic desire to take land [fewer people means a] better justification for imperialism.”
Australia was colonised on the basis of terra nullius, that it belonged to no one. That concept was overthrown with the high court’s Mabo decision, when it was recognised that First Nations people had been here for tens of thousands of years.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were not properly counted in the census until 1971, after the 1967 referendum. At that point, 115,953 people identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander.
In 2021, 812,728 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were counted in the census, a figure revised upwards to 983,257 with post-census recounts.
The estimate of 2.2 million, as well as a new estimate of 2.06 million excess deaths between 1788 and 1861, means the population was reduced to about 7% of its original size.
“We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonisation but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story,” distinguished professor Larissa Behrendt said. A Euahleyai/Gamillaroi woman, she is also the chair of the CIEHF’s advisory committee.
Early on after colonisation, various people estimated how many Aboriginal people were in their region. For example, governor Arthur Phillip estimated Gadigal people of the Eora nation came to about 1,500.
The first continent-wide estimate by social anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown put the number between 250,000 and 300,000, but mainly used observations from after the impacts of colonisation had been felt.
Radcliffe-Brown was aware that it was an underestimate, but many researchers since have relied on that count as a baseline. Again, they often recognised it would be an undercount because of historical reasons and changes in who identified or was identified as Aboriginal.
In 1983, economic historian Noel Butlin estimated the population at about 900,000. Later he increased that to between 1.1 million and 1.3 million. In 1987, archaeologists John Mulvaney and J Peter White argued it was more likely 750,000.

Before we go, let’s take a look at the day’s top headlines:
Pauline Hanson has offered a qualified apology for her comments about Indigenous Australians and about Anthony Albanese’s mother – both which have been widely condemned.
Universities Australia has warned One Nation’s plan to drastically cut down international student numbers will lead to campuses shutting down and domestic students missing out.
Australian fashion brands Cue and Veronika Maine face collapse
Longtime Australian fashion brands Cue and Veronika Maine are facing collapse after being placed under the control of receivers and managers.
The company’s parent said the decision followed “a difficult period”.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Hilco Capital said:
It is a disappointing outcome, but the only available course of action given the circumstances.
Our intention has always been to fund Cue to restore growth and profitability. This appointment will now provide an opportunity for a new owner to carry the Cue and Veronika Maine brands forward.
I want to acknowledge the efforts of all the staff during a challenging period and thank them for their continuing support of these great Australian fashion brands.
Human Rights Commission condemns Hanson’s comments about Indigenous Australians
The Australian Human Rights Commission has joined widespread condemnation of Pauline Hanson’s offensive comments about Indigenous Australians.
The commission said the comments contradicted Australia’s shared values of “fairness, dignity and respect” and had “no place in the national conversation”.
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander social justice commissioner, Katie Kiss, said:
Such commentary is a tactic to divide us at a time when we need to come together. In fact, people have come together over the past 24 hours, across the political spectrum, to criticise the senator’s comments.
For that, I am heartened. But the harm caused should not be underestimated.
The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, added:
Whether our ancestors arrived more than 200 years ago, or we are recent migrants, we all live on lands and waters that were maintained by and hold the cultures of First Peoples. Recognising that gives us strength and brings us together. Denigrating First Peoples does the opposite and lessens all of us.
When public figures use language that dehumanises entire groups of people, it causes real harm. History has shown that when people are portrayed as less deserving of dignity, respect or belonging, discrimination and exclusion are more likely to follow.
Sivaraman said the incident reinforced the commission’s recommendation in the National Anti-Racism Framework for anti-racism training for all parliamentarians.
King accuses Hanson of ‘gaslighting’ Indigenous Australians and prime minister
The resources minister, Madeleine King, has accused the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, of “gaslighting” Indigenous Australians and the prime minister after Hanson offered a qualified apology for comments that have been widely condemned.
Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, King said Hanson’s apology was inadequate. She said:
There is a way of apologising, isn’t there? … ‘Sorry if I caused offence’ is not really an apology.
She says outrageous things about Indigenous Australians, disgusting things, and then walks back into this building and says she did not say it at all. That is gaslighting.
What she said about the prime minister’s much-loved mother is beyond the pale, and a pseudo-apology is just pathetic on her behalf.
NSW police watchdog delays public examinations into alleged protest brutality investigation
The NSW independent police watchdog, the law enforcement conduct commission (Lecc), has delayed public examinations into its investigation of alleged police brutality, citing “a range of procedural issues”.

items.title: Zelenskyy's comparison of Canada to Ukraine is imperfect — but it matters
items.body_text:
Zelenskyy's comparison of Canada to Ukraine is imperfect — but it matters
Canada is confronting an unsettling truth: Powerful neighbours can rewrite the rules
There was something extraordinarily refreshing about listening to Volodymyr Zelenskyy say the quiet part out loud.
Asked to comment on the deteriorating relationship between Canada and the United States, the Ukrainian president described it as "strange" and "very dangerous" before drawing — arguably — an imperfect comparison with his country and Russia.
"It's very dangerous that there are some problems between neighbours. We are the example," Zelenskyy told CBC's chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault in an exclusive interview at the end of his visit to Canada last week.
It's well known Zelenskyy has little patience for diplomatic euphemism and he has made something of a habit of dragging the unspoken into the open.
But is it a fair and accurate comparison?
Talk to most Canadians and many are inclined to agree with the analogy at least on the surface, especially with the collapse of trade talks where Washington introduced last-minute demands — including a veto over Canada's third-party trade deals and a weakening of domestic cultural protections.
There is an important distinction, of course.
Russia invaded Ukraine.
The United States has not threatened Canada militarily and no American divisions are assembling at the border. There is no Canadian territory that's been annexed.
The Ukrainian president was quick to urge Ottawa and Washington to keep the dialogue going to work out their differences, but three times referred to the ongoing trade war and the associated rhetoric as "dangerous."
You won't find a Canadian political leader or senior official making the same comparison, at least in public.

In some of his language, Prime Minister Mark Carney alludes to it, saying how U.S. President Donald Trump "wants to break us, so he can own us."
But he never completes the thought the way Zelenskyy did.
Former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland, who remains an economic adviser to Zelenskyy, has described the Trump administration as an "existential threat" to Canada's future, but never crossed into the territory of comparing the plight of her ancestral homeland with Canada.
Even former prime minister Jean Chrétien, in his fiery, "we bow to know no one" 9/11 speech last Friday, didn't make the link.
One of the prominent Canadian voices to make the comparison is former vice-chief of the defence staff, retired vice-admiral Mark Norman.
Writing in the National Post during the early 2025 annexation controversy, Norman posed the question: "Are we as Canadians any different than Ukraine is to Russia or Taiwan to China?"

In a subsequent interview with CBC's Front Burner, the former commander of the navy used his initial argument as the jumping-off point to examine what Trump's threats meant for Canadian sovereignty.
His message was: While an American invasion is not imminent, the annexation rhetoric and the way the trade war has unfolded should force Canadians to reconsider their assumptions.
What happens when you live beside a vastly more powerful neighbour that starts to treat your sovereignty as conditional?

In a March 2025 analysis story examining Trump's 51st state rhetoric, The Washington Post asked outright: "As Putin sees Ukraine … Trump sees Canada?"
The argument was that Russian President Vladimir Putin's relationship with Ukraine provides a disturbing parallel for Trump's rhetoric toward Canada.

items.title: UN rights chief says uncovered remains in Gaza raise concerns of war crimes
items.summary: The recovery of hundreds of bodies from the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes in Gaza during the war that began nearly three years ago has raised fresh concerns about possible war crimes, the United Nations human rights chief said on Tuesday.
items.body_text:
UN rights chief says uncovered remains in Gaza raise concerns of war crimes
Volker Türk calls for full access in Gaza for international investigators to help preserve evidence
The recovery of hundreds of bodies from the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes in Gaza during the war that began nearly three years ago has raised fresh concerns about possible war crimes, the United Nations human rights chief said Tuesday.
Volker Türk said the remains of what appeared to be entire families were being unearthed from sites destroyed during Israeli attacks, adding that many victims were women and children.
"It is heartbreaking that the loved ones of those missing for so long are only now having their worst fears confirmed," he said in a statement.
He said the discoveries revived concerns raised in a 2024 UN report that found Israeli strikes on residential buildings and other civilian sites during the early weeks of the war may have violated international humanitarian law.
The Israeli Prime Minister's Office and Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations that it deliberately targets civilians and says it acted in accordance with international law while fighting Hamas militants in Gaza.
Israel's assault on Gaza — launched after Hamas's deadly raid into Israel in October 2023 — has generated around 61 million tons of wreckage and debris that could take seven years to clear, according to the United Nations.
A U.S.-brokered ceasefire brought an end to full-scale fighting in October 2025, but has failed to halt regular Israeli strikes, as both sides accuse each other of violating the truce.
The Palestinian Civil Defence says more than 630 bodies and human remains have been recovered from beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza since November 2025.
Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 people remain buried in the wreckage.
Türk said he feared the remains recovered so far could be "only the tip of the iceberg," noting that large parts of Gaza had been flattened by Israeli bombing or later demolition and clearance operations.
He also accused Israel of continuing to level some areas of Gaza where its forces remain deployed, saying bulldozers were operating "with no respect for the dead under the rubble."
The 2023 Hamas-led attacks killed 1,200 people in Israel while another 251 were taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies.
More than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel's military campaign, according to Gaza health authorities.
- Israeli strike kills 2 people in Gaza, medics say
- Israeli clearance of Gaza rubble could destroy evidence of 'atrocity crimes,' says UN expert
Israel says it has gone to great lengths to avoid civilian casualties and that Hamas uses Gaza's civilians as human shields in densely populated areas — an accusation Hamas denies.
The UN rights chief called for international investigators to be granted access to all parts of Gaza to help preserve evidence, citing ongoing legal proceedings examining conduct during the war.
Israel has blocked the entry of heavy machinery needed to remove rubble, according to Türk's statement.
Francesca Albanese, the UN expert on the Palestinian territories, has said evidence should be gathered and human remains identified before full clearance starts.
This month, the Palestinian Civil Defence said 96 bodies and human remains had been recovered from a single site in the Zeitoun area of Gaza City, including 58 children and 23 women.

items.summary: An Italian NATO fighter jet shot down a drone over Lithuania ‌shortly after midnight on Tuesday morning, the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre said.
items.body_text:
NATO fighter jet shoots down drone over Lithuania
Russia and Ukraine ignore Trump's plea to not attack energy infrastructure amid ongoing war
An Italian NATO fighter jet shot down a drone over Lithuania shortly after midnight on Tuesday morning, the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre said.
The drone, which was likely to have entered from Belarus, was shot down near Pratkunai village in southern Lithuania, near Kaunas, the second-largest city, the centre's spokesperson said. Its origin had yet to be determined, he said.
Military drones straying into the airspace of Russia's neighbours have stoked concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over NATO's borders.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said that strikes close to the alliance's territory would drive the trans-Atlantic organization to increase its support for Kyiv. Rutte also pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defences along its long eastern border with Russia.
Officials did not say whether the drone was believed to be Ukrainian or Russian. In recent months, Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace in the Baltic region. Kyiv says they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming.
A drone alert was issued earlier in the capital Vilnius and surrounding region.
The Lithuanian army shared video from the site of the crash, showing debris scattered in grass. Some of the parts appeared to be made from wood and some appeared charred.
Fighters with the NATO Baltic Air Defence mission have patrolled the skies of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia since the Baltic countries joined the alliance in 2004. The mission's jets shot down stray Ukrainian drones over Estonia in May, and over Latvia in June and August.
Denmark reports encounter with Russian ship
Separately, Denmark said a Russian frigate fired two flares towards a Danish military helicopter on Monday. Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen called the incident "unacceptable" and said it could have endangered human lives.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident was serious but not surprising, calling it part of a pattern in which an increasingly aggressive Russia has intensified its hybrid warfare against Europe and is testing NATO.
The Baltic Sea region is on high alert after incidents involving gas pipeline outages, airspace violations and drone sightings.
Russia has dismissed accusations over such incidents and repeatedly denied carrying out hybrid attacks in Europe.
Russia accused Danish military helicopters of making dangerous manoeuvres near its warships in the Baltic Sea and handed an official note to Copenhagen complaining about such incidents, Russia's ambassador to Denmark said Tuesday, according to Russia's RIA state news agency.
RIA cited Ambassador Vladimir Barbin as blaming Denmark for the episode.
Ukraine reports deaths
Meanwhile, Russia hit petrol stations in Kyiv on Tuesday and Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery, as the warring sides carried on with strikes on each other's energy targets despite an announcement on social media by U.S. President Donald Trump the previous day that they had agreed to stop.
Russia launched 200 drones at Ukraine's capital and other cities in overnight attacks, killing two people. In addition to the petrol stations in Kyiv, it struck energy and port infrastructure in other regions, Ukrainian officials said.

items.summary: Air Force Secretary says the U.S. has fielded ‘on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action’
items.body_text:
The United States has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told the Air and Space Cyber Conference in Maryland on Monday that the U.S. has fielded “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.”
Meink did not detail what the weapons were or how they work. In 2024 the U.S. said Russia was developing a new anti-satellite weapon that could be launched from space. At the time the White House said the danger wasn’t imminent.
But reports of the anti-satellite weapon reflected longstanding worries about space threats from Russia and China, given that much U.S. infrastructure is dependent on satellite communications.
In his remarks, Meink also said the Air Force was adding more autonomous systems to its capabilities and predicted the service would look “radically different” by 2032. For example, he foresaw one-way attack drones replacing artillery as the “primary killer.”
“We are increasing readiness against existing threats,” he said.
Trump created the Space Force in 2019.

items.title: FBI Director Kash Patel to face U.S. Senate grilling over travel, 2020 election probe
items.summary: He could also face questions over his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation
items.body_text:
FBI Director Kash Patel is set to face the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday, when Democrats are expected to grill him over his leadership, use of taxpayer funds for personal travel and claims that arrests were imminent related to the 2020 election.
Republicans will likely ask about probes into the federal investigation of attempts to overturn that presidential election, an issue Republican committee chair Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa has said is a top priority for the committee.
Tuesday’s appearance comes days after Joe DiGenova, who had been leading an investigation scrutinizing several of Trump’s foes and that sought to prove the president was the victim of a criminal conspiracy, abruptly resigned last week. Patel will likely receive questions over the implications and reasons behind DiGenova’s departure.
It will be Patel’s first appearance before the Senate since May, when Democrats pressed him over a media report that the FBI director’s excessive drinking had interfered with his ability to lead the premier U.S. law enforcement agency. Patel defended his leadership and denied the report, arguing he has helped reduce crime nationwide.
Patel has since appeared with Trump to tout the lowest levels of violent crime in decades, a trend that had begun before Trump’s second term.
Patel has also forged an unprecedented partnership with China and Russia to combat transnational crime, Reuters previously reported, a program that critics say is dangerous and could undermine U.S. national security.
Patel has been the near-constant subject of controversy since he took over the FBI.
He drew criticism over media reports about him scuba diving at a Pearl Harbor memorial, and for drinking beer while celebrating with the gold-medal-winning U.S. men’s hockey team at the Milan Winter Olympics.
That scrutiny has at times come from Republicans, including Grassley, who sought information in a May 5 letter about Patel’s use of a government plane, luxury cars and other taxpayer funds, according to the top Democrats on the House and Senate Judiciary committees.
Patel could also face questions over his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation, including about recently released texts showing Patel ordering a top aide to respond to anonymous social media accounts mocking that effort.

On the map: Kerr Village Towns fill ‘missing middle ground’ in South Oakville
Development addresses neighbourhood’s most glaring shortcoming — a lack of housing beyond detached homes and condos
We independently select everything we recommend. Buying through us may earn us a commission, which supports our work.
Home to various restaurants, boutiques and parks, and steps from Lake Ontario, South Oakville’s Kerr Village has no shortage of appealing urban amenities. But according to Noah Shechtman, director of development at Brightstone, it is the affluent neighbourhood’s most glaring shortcoming — a lack of housing beyond detached homes and condos — that’s drawing prospective buyers to Kerr Village Towns.
“Detached homes in mature neighbourhoods can be difficult to access for many buyers, while condo living may not meet the needs of those looking for more private space, parking or a traditional residential layout,” he says. “Kerr Village Towns is designed to fill that missing middle ground.”
Planned for the northwest corner of Garden Drive and Lakeshore Road, the four-storey community features four blocks of units: 42 back-to-back townhomes each spanning approximately 1,800 square feet, six 2,000-square-foot townhomes, and two commercial units on Lakeshore. Brightstone is currently building a sales centre on Lakeshore, with a broader public sales launch expected to follow.
Together, the homes are being presented as a boutique infill project shaped by its prime South Oakville setting. “We wanted to bring more luxury home ownership to South Oakville,” Shechtman says. “We say ‘luxury by the lake’ because we’re a five-minute walk to the lake, and we’re just a quick stroll to downtown Oakville, the yacht club and the marina.”
The project is designed by Toronto-based architect Richard Wengle, who says in the project brochure that he found inspiration in “the character of South Oakville,” including its “opulence and grandeur,” and blended that with “the contemporary urban energy” of Kerr Village. The result is a low-rise enclave with traditional detailing, oversized windows, formal rooflines and a streetscape presence intended to complement the surrounding neighbourhood.
Inside, the homes include open kitchens, formal dining areas, large windows, electric fireplaces, custom cabinetry, spa-inspired bathrooms and private elevators. Shechtman says feedback from registrants helped confirm the importance of those features, particularly for buyers moving from larger homes.
The typical buyer, he adds, is expected to be a downsizer who wants to sell a single-detached home but avoid condo living. “They want the same type of homeownership feel — front door, rooftop terrace, separate-level living — but also want to stay in South Oakville.”
That buyer profile influenced the design and feature package. “We needed to include private elevators for every unit,” Shechtman says. Brightstone has also introduced car lifts, giving every home two-car parking. Other features include quartz countertops, 10-foot ceilings, pot lights, built-in fireplaces and EV rough-ins.
The anticipated buyer profile also includes younger professional couples seeking more space, parking, storage and flexibility than a condo can provide, without moving into a pricier detached home. Shechtman says Kerr Village Towns is coming to market at a lower price point than some luxury townhomes in South Oakville, making it a different form of ownership for the area.
“There’s already a lot of luxury living in South Oakville,” he says. “But we wanted to bring even more homes, because they’re needed.” Rather than offering townhomes priced above $3 million, he says, Brightstone sought to introduce homes closer to $1.5 million to appeal to young couples and downsizers.

items.title: Alberta’s separatists have a Mark Carney problem
items.summary: The prime minister's rising popularity comes at an inopportune time for separatists: 'Our biggest salespeople have always been the Liberals,' one advocate says
items.body_text:
Alberta's separatists have a Mark Carney problem
The prime minister's rising popularity comes at an inopportune time for separatists: 'Our biggest salespeople have always been the Liberals,' one advocate says
In late 2024, Alberta’s separatists were riding high on a wave of anti-Trudeau sentiment. Public support for the Liberal government had hit fresh lows, and a decade of activist policymaking under the former prime minister had reinforced the province’s longtime skepticism that Ottawa could properly represent its interests.
Two years on, some Alberta separatists say that Prime Minister Mark Carney’s growing popularity among Canadians — as well as a new oil pipeline deal between Ottawa and Alberta — have likely changed the calculus for many voters ahead of the province’s October referendum.
“If Justin Trudeau had stayed in power, I’m quite sure we would have been able to (separate),” said Michael Wagner, a committed separatist and author of ‘No Other Option: Self-Determination for Alberta.’ “Because Mark Carney is trying to extend an olive branch, that’s kind of hurting our cause.”
Wagner, who was partaking in a pro-separatism event in Calgary this weekend called “Capitalism & Morality,” was reflecting the views of many staunch separatists in attendance. While Carney’s efforts to appease Alberta haven’t convinced the separatist movement’s core supporters, people said, the swing in popularity could be enough to nudge more neutral voters away from outright separation.
“It’s reverse psychology, but our biggest salespeople have always been the Liberals,” Wagner said.
A new Leger poll puts Carney’s support at 49 per cent in September, up three points from a month earlier. That widens the gap over Pierre Poilievre’s Conservatives, which Leger put one point lower, at 33 per cent. It’s a sharp reversal of Liberal fortunes from late 2024 and early 2025, when Trudeau’s support had slumped to just over 20 per cent, according to various polls at the time.
Much of Carney’s growing support is a result of U.S. President Donald Trump’s taunts against Canada, both in matters of trade and sovereignty, which have galvanized federalist sentiments among Canadian voters.
In November, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Carney that includes a promise to build a new one-million-barrel-per-day pipeline to the B.C. coast, among other energy-related policies and targets.
The roughly $40-billion project, led by federal Crown agency Trans Mountain Corp., still needs to overcome a long list of political and legal hurdles before it is completed. The pipeline still has no private sector company to lead the development, and doesn’t yet have the right-of-way to build a proposed terminal on the B.C. coast, south of Vancouver.
Drew Barnes, a former United Conservative Party member who was ousted from Jason Kenney’s caucus in 2021, said there are various headwinds facing the separatist movement. Smith’s increasingly vocal support for Alberta remaining in Canada is one, he said, as well as a “fragmented” media landscape that has stifled pro-independence voices.
“It’s a hard road now to get a message out,” he said.
Barnes, for his part, said he didn’t think that separatist support has lessened in recent months, but nonetheless acknowledged that the pace of growth has slowed since the closure of the pro-independence petition.
“I don’t think it’s waned, but it hasn’t grown with the momentum it started with,” he said.

items.title: My darling 16-year-old daughter has turned into a monster and I’m terrified | Ask Rebecca
items.summary: Nature did not design adolescence with mothers’ feelings high on the priority list. Your daughter can be struggling and still be expected to say hello
items.body_text:
My darling 16-year-old daughter has turned into a monster and I'm terrified | Ask Rebecca
Nature did not design adolescence with mothers’ feelings high on the priority list. Your daughter can be struggling and still be expected to say hello
Ask Rebecca is smart, honest advice to readers’ questions about life, family and relationships by columnist Rebecca Eckler. Got a question for Rebecca? Submit it anonymously on the form here. You can also send an email to NPadvice@postmedia.com.
Dear Rebecca:
Recommended Videos
My incredible 16-year-old daughter has turned into a monster. From birth until 14, she was kind, lovable, helpful, understanding and an amazing person. I’m a single mother, and it’s just the two of us, but we managed to live together peacefully and happily. I work extremely hard to earn enough to pay the rent, bills and necessities. She’s always been grateful.
Two years ago, she called me at work and said she wanted to hurt herself. I took her to the hospital immediately. After that, she started showing small signs of anger and frustration, but nothing we couldn’t handle. When she’d get upset, she’d come to me, and we’d talk it out.
But when she needed parenting, I was often too delicate, afraid to upset her and make her depressed again. Now she’s constantly sulking around, won’t clean her room, won’t help with chores, won’t talk to me at all, won’t not even say hello. She refuses to speak to any professional. She claims she’s fine, but she’s not.
I’m upset, tired, and frustrated. Worst of all, I’m terrified of saying something that will send her over the edge. Please tell me this changes — I miss my darling daughter so much.— Mother on Eggshells
Dear Mother on Eggshells:
First, I don’t think your daughter is a monster.
I think she’s 16. And I say that with enormous compassion for anyone living with one right now. Sixteen-year-olds are not an easy species to live with.
I should also say the obvious but important thing. I’m an advice columnist, not a mental-health professional. If at any point you believe your daughter is in immediate danger of harming herself, call 911 or get her to the nearest ER.
There are few things more upsetting than having a child who once demanded you hug her while she did #2 suddenly behave as if your chewing is an irritating habit you’ve developed just to annoy her. But something more complicated is happening here. It started with the phone call no parent ever wants to receive. Your 14-year-old daughter called you at work and told you she wanted to hurt herself.
Of course you took her seriously and rushed her to the hospital. But I think you brought something home with you that day, too.
Fear.
Once your child tells you something like that, it changes the way you hear every slammed door, every silence and every just leave me alone.
For the last two years, you haven’t just been parenting a teenager. You’ve been parenting one while carrying around the terrifying knowledge that she had once been in enough pain to consider hurting herself.
Somewhere along the way, fear turned into a family dynamic in which your daughter’s unhappiness became something you feel responsible for preventing.
You can’t.
You are responsible for taking her mental health seriously and paying attention. But you are not responsible for making sure your 16-year-old is never angry, frustrated, disappointed or pissed off at her mother.
There is also a difference between mental health struggles and unacceptable behaviour. The first deserves compassion. The second requires boundaries. Sulking is behaviour. Refusing chores is behaviour. Being rude is behaviour. Not wanting to talk to your mother is extremely irritating, but also fairly common behaviour.
Stop forcing her into appointments. Clearly that isn’t getting you anywhere. If she won’t go, you go instead. Find someone who understands adolescents and tell them exactly what you’ve said here. You need someone who can help you distinguish between “I’m 16, leave me alone” and “I

items.title: «Le Québec est au centre de la transformation de l’économie», dit Eric Girard à Toronto
items.summary: Le ministre des Finances du Québec participe au Sommet canadien de l’investissement du premier ministre Carney.
items.body_text:
Le ministre des Finances du Québec, Eric Girard, porte le message, en participant au sommet visant à stimuler l’investissement privé qui a lieu à Toronto, que « le Québec est au centre de la transformation de l’économie canadienne ».
« On a un important secteur manufacturier. On a de l’énergie propre, on a de l’expertise en défense. On a des minéraux critiques et stratégiques », a-t-il énuméré en entrevue téléphonique, depuis la Ville Reine.
Le ministre portera une oreille attentive, tout au long de la journée de mardi, aux différents panels de discussion prévus, mais participera aussi aux conversations de couloir et autres événements informels.
Arrivé à Toronto lundi, il a confié à La Presse canadienne qu’il était enthousiaste quant à la brochette d’investisseurs étrangers présents et qui sont largement considérés comme le gratin du monde des affaires.
« Ici sont réunis des représentants des entreprises privées, des intermédiaires financiers, les grandes institutions financières, les gouvernements, les promoteurs des projets, mais l’élément clé, ce sont les investisseurs étrangers qui viennent ici pour étudier ces projets-là », a-t-il dit.
Tout comme le premier ministre fédéral, Mark Carney, M. Girard déplore un déficit en matière d’investissements privés au Canada et au Québec.
Il note que cet enjeu remonte à bien avant l’actuelle guerre commerciale qui ébranle bien des entreprises, de même que le retour de Donald Trump à la Maison-Blanche.
Des investisseurs qui ont répondu présents à l’invitation au sommet du gouvernement fédéral, comme BlackRock, auront l’occasion de se faire présenter une foule de projets canadiens et québécois.
BlackRock est considéré comme le premier gestionnaire d’actifs en importance mondialement.
« Ces projets-là, ce qu’ils ont tous en commun, c’est qu’ils sont intensifs en capital — ça prend beaucoup de capitaux — et il y a aussi beaucoup d’incertitude quant aux prix au moment où ces projets-là vont être réalisés », a dit le ministre québécois.
Il a évoqué des projets qui se déploieraient « à coups de milliards ».
« Le gouvernement du Québec est un catalyseur, c’est-à-dire qu’il est prêt à mettre des sommes pour que ces projets-là soient initiés, mais notre degré d’intervention doit être limité et diversifié, d’où la nécessité d’avoir plus de capitaux privés et plus de capitaux étrangers pour que ce soit eux, les capitaux privés, qui prennent la majorité des risques de ces projets-là qui sont, à la base, des projets risqués, mais des projets importants pour l’économie du Québec. »
Le ministre Girard représente le gouvernement du Québec au Sommet canadien de l’investissement auquel ont convergé des centaines de dirigeants d’entreprises.
Selon la liste des participants fournie par le bureau du premier ministre Carney, de grands joueurs du monde des affaires au Québec seront représentés, comme Bombardier, le groupe Desjardins et Rio Tinto, société qui est notamment un ténor dans le secteur de l’aluminium au Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean.
Rio Tinto envoie à l’événement son président du conseil Dominic Barton, qui a été à la tête du groupe conseil McKinsey ayant travaillé auprès de nombreux gouvernements, de même qu’ambassadeur du Canada en Chine.
M. Barton porte aussi le chapeau de président du conseil d’administration d’une organisation créée par le gouvernement Carney qui s’appelle Investir au Canada, une initiative qui vise à mobiliser des investissements du secteur privé.
La dirigeante de la société d’État Hydro-Québec, Claudine Bouchard, sera aussi présente mardi, toujours selon la liste, de même que le président et chef de la direction de La Caisse, Charles Émond.
L’événement n’est pas sans rappeler un « sommet » qui avait été initié par l’ex-premier ministre Justin Trudeau en février 2025, appelé le Sommet Canada-États-Unis, et qui avait aussi eu lieu à Toronto.
Mais selon le ministre Girard, c’est une première au chapitre de réussir à rassembler autant de grands investisseurs reconnus mondialement.
Né

items.title: Clément Hervieu-Léger, l’avenir de la Comédie-Française
items.summary: L’administrateur général parle du rôle que le Québec pourrait tenir dans l’avenir de la prestigieuse compagnie qu’il dirige.
items.body_text:
Clément Hervieu-Léger a été nommé administrateur général de la Comédie-Française le 4 août 2025. De passage à Montréal à l’occasion de la tournée québécoise et canadienne de Lumières, lumières, lumières, la pièce d’Evelyne de la Chenelière mise en scène par Florent Siaud avec deux actrices de la Maison de Molière, Florence Viala et Aymeline Alix, le comédien, metteur en scène et pédagogue, à la tête d’une troupe permanente de 57 comédiens et comédiennes, a pris le temps de nous parler de tradition, mais aussi d’innovation et du rôle que le Québec pourrait occuper dans ses plans d’avenir.
Cette première coproduction avec une compagnie québécoise, Les songes turbulents, que dirige Florent Siaud, Clément Hervieu-Léger la considère comme une manière pour la Comédie-Française, qui existe depuis 1680, ce qui en fait la troupe en activité la plus ancienne au monde, d’« aller vers le public ». « Comme institution, je trouve que c’est essentiel de ne pas seulement attendre que le public vienne à nous. C’était donc nécessaire, pour moi, d’être ici. Je n’aurais pas imaginé que ce spectacle soit ici, que la Comédie-Française soit à Montréal et au Québec, sans que l’administrateur général soit présent. »
Clément Hervieu-Léger, qui était de la distribution de Lucrèce Borgia, un spectacle que la Comédie-Française a présenté au théâtre du Nouveau Monde à l’été 2017, à l’occasion des festivités du 375e anniversaire de Montréal, tenait à revenir dans la métropole et à rencontrer des artistes et des artisans d’ici. « Le Québec, c’est et ce doit être un interlocuteur privilégié pour la Comédie-Française. C’est pourquoi ça m’importait de venir à la rencontre des gens, des directeurs, des directrices, mais aussi d’aller voir des lieux, d’avoir une vision un peu plus précise de la cartographie théâtrale québécoise. Je suis très ouvert à l’idée d’imaginer de nouvelles formes de collaboration. Il y a plein de choses qui sont possibles, que ce soient des coproductions, des accueils ou que sais-je encore. La création de Lumières, lumières, lumières en est la preuve. »
Plans d’avenir
Le mandat de Clément Hervieu-Léger est de cinq ans. Sa première année en poste n’a pas été de tout repos, notamment à cause de travaux importants réalisés dans la salle Richelieu, celle que la troupe occupe depuis 1799, la plus grande des trois salles dont dispose la Comédie-Française. « Les travaux sont terminés, annonce fièrement l’administrateur général. Toutes les équipes sont revenues, et les spectacles vont reprendre à partir du 15 octobre. »
                                                    « Comme institution, je trouve que c’est essentiel de ne pas seulement attendre que le public vienne à nous. C’était donc nécessaire, pour moi, d’être ici [au Québec]. »
Clément Hervieu-Léger
Photo: Marie-France Coallier Le Devoir
L’un des chevaux de bataille de l’homme, c’est le rapport au répertoire. « On se doit de l’interroger, explique-t-il. Il faut s’interdire de le concevoir comme une bibliothèque un peu muséale de textes anciens qu’on continuerait à jouer sans trop savoir pourquoi. Est-ce que les pièces qui nous arrivent du XVIIe et du XVIIIe siècles, qu’on a beaucoup jouées, continuent à être pertinentes pour éclairer le monde contemporain ? Le répertoire, c’est un bien commun qui doit s’enrichir, qui doit être malaxé. »
Clément Hervieu-Léger tient à ce que la maison qu’il dirige « demeure en phase avec le monde qui l’entoure ». « Le théâtre, c’est l’occasion de faire l’expérience de notre commune humanité, mais aussi celle de trouver des clés pour appréhender un monde qui est sacrément complexe et parfois très angoissant. » Pour l’administrateur, être de son temps, ça passe notamment par l’espace accordé aux femmes. « On n’a pas toujours, à la Comédie-Française, donné aux autrices la place qui leur revient. items.title: Le problème de l’incroyance
items.summary: La perte de confiance envers l’État va-t-elle finir par transformer en vertu l’austérité autrefois honnie?
items.body_text:
Depuis les années Couillard, le mot « austérité » a été banni du vocabulaire politique québécois, sauf quand il s’agit d’en faire le reproche à un adversaire. Après la corruption, c’est peut-être le pire péché dont on peut l’accuser.
En présentant le cadre financier de son parti, le chef du Parti libéral du Québec, Charles Milliard, a déclaré que ce mot ne lui faisait pas peur, même s’il préférait parler de « réalisme économique », comme d’autres se sont réclamés de la « rigueur » ou de la « responsabilité », mais les électeurs ont appris à ne pas se laisser berner par les synonymes.
Quand on parle d’une augmentation des dépenses limitée à 1 % entre 2028 et 2030, soit bien en deçà de l’inflation, ils savent très bien ce que cela signifie. Même le gouvernement Couillard n’avait pas été aussi pingre. M. Milliard affirme que les réseaux de la santé et de l’éducation seront épargnés, mais la population est arrivée depuis longtemps à la conclusion qu’ils se dégraderont, peu importe l’argent qu’on y investit, malgré les progrès que veulent rapporter les graphiques et les tableaux de bord.
Il ne faut pas s’étonner que deux Québécois sur trois préfèrent une réduction des services publics à une hausse d’impôt, selon un sondage effectué par Léger cet été pour la Chaire en fiscalité et en finances publiques. En réalité, ils craignent d’avoir à la fois moins de services et plus d’impôt à payer. Tant qu’à faire, aussi bien en avoir pour son argent en se tournant vers le privé.
***
Pendant des années, le filet social mis en place pendant la Révolution tranquille a fait la fierté des Québécois. Ce sentiment semble de plus en faire place à une incroyance en la compétence de l’État, voire en son intégrité, ce qui est de très mauvais augure pour ce qu’on appelait jadis la « société juste ». Qui sait, l’austérité va peut-être devenir une vertu.
Les partis d’opposition se sont empressés de présenter comme un scandale caquiste l’explosion des coûts du Système d’information des finances et de l’approvisionnement (SIFA) de Santé Québec révélée par Radio-Canada lundi. Et Christine Fréchette en paiera peut-être le prix le 5 octobre, mais c’est l’État lui-même qui s’en trouve un peu plus discrédité.
Il n’y a pas de « poudre magique » dans le cadre financier du PLQ, et son chef s’en est presque félicité. S’il entendait par là que les nouvelles dépenses seront réduites au minimum, on peut en dire autant du cadre déjà présenté par la Coalition avenir Québec, et celui que le Parti québécois dévoilera au cours des prochaines heures sera sans doute de la même eau.
Réalisme oblige, les engagements d’un gouvernement Milliard pour le prochain mandat totaliseraient 11,9 milliards de dollars, par rapport aux 41 milliards que Dominique Anglade promettait en 2022. Le cadre financier présenté par Christine Fréchette prévoit des engagements de 9,7 milliards de dollars, par rapport à 30,6 milliards il y a quatre ans. Dans le cas du PQ, ce chiffre était de 29,7 milliards.
Le Parti conservateur du Québec nous fait évidemment entrer dans une autre dimension avec sa proposition de compressions de 47 milliards de dollars. Penser que cela pourrait se faire sans influer sur les services, comme le prétend son chef, Éric Duhaime, tient de la fantasmagorie. On parle ici d’un État croupion et du triomphe de l’incroyance.
***
Québec solidaire est aujourd’hui le seul parti à prendre la défense du « modèle québécois ». Et avec un cadre financier qui prévoit quatre fois moins de nouvelles dépenses que celui de 2022, on est bien loin de la nationalisation de grands pans de l’économie que le parti ambitionnait jadis.
Contrairement aux autres, QS n’envisage pas la moindre réduction dans les effectifs de la fonction publique (que certains présentent comme un repaire de parasites). Il propose au contraire de les augmenter, notamment pour redonner à l’État l’expertise dont le cafouillage à répétition des projets de transformation numérique a démontré la nécessité.

items.title: The National Palace’s new resident has four legs and one role: to support emotional well-being
items.summary: Rollo, a mixed breed, will have plenty of room to do what he likes best: run around. But he'll have to share the palace grounds with some long-established residents... somewhere close to 20 cats. The post The National Palace’s new resident has four legs and one role: to support emotional well-being appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
The Mexican government has just introduced a new resident of the National Palace. And no, it’s not a politician or public official. It’s a puppy, and his name is Rollo.
In a video posted on the government’s official social media accounts, Rollo is seen running playfully through the corridors and gardens of the National Palace. In another scene, he’s behind a desk, wearing a tie.
Él es Rollo, trabaja en Palacio Nacional. Es un cachorro mestizo adoptado que hoy se divierte en jardines y oficinas bajo el resguardo de la Dirección General de Comunicación Digital de la Presidencia. Tiene un papel muy importante: el apoyo y bienestar emocional de todas y… pic.twitter.com/aoRmKbXHlT
— Gobierno de México (@GobiernoMX) September 10, 2026
“This is Rollo. He works at the National Palace,” the post says, adding that the adopted pet, a mixed-breed, has a “very important role: the support and emotional well-being of everyone.”
The video also indicates that Rollo has a brother named Theo, who is still looking for an adoptive family. However, details of where and how to adopt him have not been shared.
Rollo joins other animals living at the National Palace, including the cats that inhabit its gardens and other areas of the palace. President Claudia Sheinbaum herself has shown off these pets during tours of the presidential headquarters.
In May 2026, during the visit of the K-pop group BTS to the National Palace, Sheinbaum said that 16 cats lived there. However, the number of these animals has varied over the years.
In 2024, it was reported that 19 cats inhabiting the National Palace were designated as “living fixed assets” — a legal measure to guarantee resources for their food, medical attention and care for the rest of their lives.
The gatos that have been publicly identified include Coco, Zeus, Roja, Ollie and Balam — two of whom have made a debut on the internet. During the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Coco appeared in posts on official government accounts wearing Mexico’s jersey. Meanwhile, Zeus once wandered into a morning press conference during Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s term (2018-2024).
Unlike Rollo, these cats were not adopted. According to information from the presidential office, they have been there for years, and there is no precise record of how each one arrived.
With reports from Infobae and El Financiero

items.title: Mexico moves toward promoting sports tourism as a major draw for international visitors
items.summary: Business and tourism leaders, both public and private, see untapped potential in packaging tourism opportunities with Mexico's stacked calendar of sporting events each year. The post Mexico moves toward promoting sports tourism as a major draw for international visitors appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
Fresh off hosting the fourth World Sports Tourism Congress that attracted 500 participants from 30 countries, Mexico is developing a campaign to turn sports tourism into a major draw for visitors.
Spearheaded by the Confederation of National Chambers of Commerce, Services and Tourism (Concanaco Servytur), the project will get support from the public sector, including the Association of Tourism Secretaries of Mexico (Asetur), the federal Tourism Ministry and state sports institutes, all aiming to develop broader tourist experiences around national and international sports competitions.
For starters, Concanaco is developing Mexico’s 2027 sports tourism calendar to enhance the country’s potential for attracting tourists via sporting events.
Mexico is the first Latin American country to host the World Sports Tourism Congress, which ran from Sept. 7 to 9, and is already rich in major sporting events. Concanaco will identify existing championships or tournaments and promote additional tourism activities in the destinations where they are held.
“These aren’t new tournaments; they already exist and are held in the country,” Concanaco President Octavio de la Torre said in an interview with the newspaper EFE, referring to the events on the calendar. “But we’re going to make them visible as sports tourism, not just as a sporting activity. In this ecosystem, we’re going to connect experiences with lodging and, of course, commerce.”
The northeastern border state of Tamaulipas in particular is looking to establish itself as a leading destination for sports tourism. According to state Tourism Minister Benjamín Hernández Rodríguez, the state has allocated over 236 million pesos (US $13.8 million) to the improvement and construction of recreational and high-performance facilities.
Tamaulipas already hosts several major sports events, such as the upcoming Gran Fondo Tampico, a cycling event set for Sept. 27, which offers visitors not only a race to watch but also opportunities to enjoy cultural, gastronomic and recreational activities in the Gulf coast city of Tampico.
International tourism is up — at the border
Mexico received 4.41 million international tourists in July, 3.8% more than in the same month of 2025, the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) reported on Monday. The United States remained the leading source market, with 1.69 million arrivals.
However, July registered a 3.2% decline in international tourists staying at least one night while simultaneously logging a 13.2% increase in border tourism, referring to visitors who enter Mexico at its northern or southern border but do not travel farther inland. Similarly, air arrivals of international tourists in July were down 5.7%.
With reports from López-Dóriga Digital and Diario de México

items.title: Industrial activity grew 2.4% in July, its best result in nearly 3 years
items.summary: In July, industrial activity in Mexico was up 2.4% in annual seasonally adjusted terms, the sector's strongest growth since November 2023. The post Industrial activity grew 2.4% in July, its best result in nearly 3 years appeared first on Mexico News Daily
items.body_text:
Industrial activity in Mexico grew 2.4% in annual seasonally adjusted terms in July, the best result in almost three years.
Month-over-month growth was 0.5%, according to the national statistics agency INEGI, which published the data last Friday.
The construction sector was the driving force behind the annual growth, the strongest since October 2023, although the mining, manufacturing and energy sectors also made gains.
Construction activity increased 6.7% annually in July, mining activity grew 1.6% and manufacturing activity rose 1.3%. Activity related to electricity, gas and water supply increased 0.7% compared to July 2025.
On a month-over-month basis, construction activity grew 0.9% in July and manufacturing activity increased 0.7%. The electricity, gas and water sector recorded 0.0% month-over-month growth, while mining activity declined 1.8%.
The year-over-year industrial activity growth in July was triple the 0.8% reading in June. The month-over-month growth was more than double the 0.2% increase recorded in June.
Industrial activity has now increased on an annual basis across four consecutive months. July marked the second consecutive month with sequential growth in industrial activity.
Industrial activity is up slightly this year
In the first seven months of 2026, industrial activity grew 0.4% compared to the same period of last year, according to INEGI.
Mining activity increased 3.5% annually in the January-July period, while construction activity grew 2.8%.
Manufacturing activity — the largest contributor to the industrial data — declined 0.7% on a year-over-year basis while the electricity, gas and water sectors collectively recorded 0.0% annual growth.
The modest year-over-year growth between January and July came after industrial activity contracted 1.3% in 2025.
Economists from Grupo Financiero Monex said in a report that they anticipated that industrial activity would continue to grow at a “moderate” pace in the coming months.
They said that USMCA-related uncertainty and U.S. tariffs on certain strategic Mexican goods (vehicles, steel and aluminum) could continue to constrain investment decisions and the performance of export-oriented manufacturing sectors.
With reports from El Economista

os líderes de los laboratorios de inteligencia artificial (IA) más importantes están llamando a un pacto para frenar la competencia frenética en la que se ven inmersos, y estudian la creación de un organismo que se encargaría de controlar unos sistemas de IA que, según los avances logrados en lo que va de año, podrían causar estragos millonarios al “desalinearse”. En el contexto de la IA, la alineación es el proceso de diseñar y ajustar los modelos para que sus acciones, objetivos y resultados coincidan con los valores, la ética y las intenciones de los seres humanos.
El director ejecutivo de OpenAI, Sam Altman; el responsable de la unidad de IA de Google, Demis Hassabis, y el director ejecutivo de SpaceX, Elon Musk, respaldaron un ensayo publicado el sábado por su homólogo de Anthropic, Dario Amodei, en el cual éste llama a sus colegas a avanzar de manera más lenta y cautelosa en el desarrollo de esta poderosa tecnología, trabajar juntos para establecer normas de seguridad comunes y apoyar algún tipo de cooperación gubernamental sobre esta cuestión. Por su parte, Microsoft presentó un borrador de código de conducta para su IA interna que refleja la creciente preocupación del sector por la necesidad de mantener bajo control humano las potentes IA del futuro. La compañía fundada por Bill Gates aseguró que “las personas importan más que la IA”, y reafirmó su visión previa de una “superinteligencia humanista”.
Sin duda es positivo que los responsables de algunos de los modelos de IA más avanzados y los que gozan de mayor adopción en Occidente demuestren ser conscientes de los serios riesgos que entrañan sus productos. La preocupación no es gratuita: en días recientes, Anthropic anunció que bloqueó cinco intentos de científicos que usaron su inteligencia artificial Claude para investigaciones que podrían llevar a la creación de armas biológicas, mientras OpenAI –propietaria de ChatGPT– reveló que varios de sus modelos “escaparon” de un entorno confinado, se conectaron a Internet de manera autónoma e infiltraron otra empresa.
Lamentablemente, los magnates tecnológicos no destacan como referentes éticos; por el contrario, han demostrado de manera reiterada que ponen la acumulación de riqueza por encima de cualquier otra consideración. Musk bromeó con organizar un golpe de Estado en Bolivia para apropiarse del litio; durante la pandemia de covid-19 obligó a sus empleados a trabajar de manera presencial bajo amenaza de despido, y sostiene puntos de vista eugenésicos y abiertamente fascistas, como que la “gente inteligente” debe tener muchos hijos para mejorar a la humanidad. Bill Gates presionó a la Universidad de Oxford para que desistiera de sus planes de ofrecer su vacuna contra el coronavirus mediante una licencia abierta, no exclusiva y libre de regalías, y entregara la patente exclusiva a la multinacional AstraZeneca. Así, un fármaco desarrollado en 97 por ciento con fondos públicos y donados se convirtió en un multimillonario negocio privado a expensas de un número incalculable de vidas perdidas. Este año, Serguéi Brin, cofundador de Google, ha gastado al menos 120 millones de dólares para descarrilar los intentos de establecer un impuesto a los ultrarricos en California. Mark Zuckerberg, fundador de Meta (matriz de Facebook, Instagram y WhatsApp), enfrenta un juicio por implementar algoritmos a sabiendas de que eran dañinos para la salud mental de adolescentes.
El panorama empeora porque Estados Unidos, sede de todas las empresas mencionadas, está gobernado por un sujeto que no entiende nada de IA, cree saberlo todo y se encuentra obsesionado con una desregulación absoluta cuya consecuencia sería, de concretarse, la destrucción del planeta. items.title: Kansas City gana en el regreso de Mahomes
items.summary: En el regreso a los emparrillados de Patrick Mahomes luego de nueve meses de ausencia, los Jefes de Kansas City vencieron 31-10 a los Broncos de Denver en el cierre de la jornada 1 de la NFL.
items.body_text:
Martes 15 de septiembre de 2026, p. a12
En el regreso a los emparrillados de Patrick Mahomes luego de nueve meses de ausencia, los Jefes de Kansas City vencieron 31-10 a los Broncos de Denver en el cierre de la jornada 1 de la NFL.
El mariscal de campo, tres veces ganador del Supertazón y quien sufrió una rotura de ligamento cruzado anterior, consiguió una anotación por la vía terrestre y dos pases a las diagonales para encaminar a su equipo a su primera victoria.
Apenas en el primer cuarto, Mahomes consiguió los primeros puntos para los Jefes al protagonizar una gran serie ofensiva y llegar a la zona de anotación. Evan Engram logró el empate para Broncos.
En el segundo cuarto los locales retomaron la ventaja con una anotación de Rashee Rice para el 14-7. Así se fueron al descanso.
En el tercer episodio, Kansas logró llegar nuevamente a la zona prometida por conducto de Kenneth Walker. Además consiguieron dos goles de campo para ampliar su ventaja a 24-10 pues Denver también sumó tres puntos.
En el primer Monday Night Football de la temporada, los Jefes reafirmaron su dominio con una anotación más de Walker para el definitivo 31-10.
En la que podría ser su última temporada con el equipo, Travis Kelce se convirtió en el segundo ala cerrada con más yardas por recepción con 13 mil 067. Ayer consiguió 71.

items.title: Quieren borrar de la nube digital las lenguas indígenas, denuncia mixteco
items.summary: Desde la tribuna de la Cámara de Diputados, el ciudadano e integrante de la comunidad mixteca Moisés Hilario López llamó ayer a los legisladores a modificar la ley para impulsar el uso de la tecnología y la inteligencia artificial (IA), con el fin de preservar las lenguas indígenas y combatir la discriminación contra sus hablantes.
items.body_text:
Revela que los niños de su comunidad enfrentan burlas en su vida diaria y en redes sociales por su forma de hablar
Martes 15 de septiembre de 2026, p. 5
Desde la tribuna de la Cámara de Diputados, el ciudadano e integrante de la comunidad mixteca Moisés Hilario López llamó ayer a los legisladores a modificar la ley para impulsar el uso de la tecnología y la inteligencia artificial (IA), con el fin de preservar las lenguas indígenas y combatir la discriminación contra sus hablantes.
“Nos quieren borrar de la nube digital”, pronunció en lengua tu’un savi, cuya traducción se mostró en la pantalla del salón de plenos.
Ingeniero en matemáticas por el Instituto Politécnico Nacional, Hilario López participó en el ejercicio Lenguas indígenas toman la palabra, que se realiza al inicio de cada sesión.
Ante un salón semivacío y mientras buena parte de los diputados presentes desatendía su intervención, advirtió que niños mixtecos llegan a ocultar su lengua para evitar burlas; que quienes migran a las ciudades son presionados para avergonzarse de su forma de hablar, y que esa discriminación también se reproduce en las redes sociales.
“Si la inteligencia artificial puede aprender inglés, francés y alemán en un segundo, ¿por qué no le enseñan mixteco? ¿Por qué no se enseña otra lengua indígena? ¡No es falta de tecnología, es falta de voluntad política!”, exaltó.
Hilario López planteó a los legisladores asumir tres compromisos de Estado. El primero, mencionó, consiste en destinar programas y presupuesto para crear archivos digitales vivos de las lenguas originarias y utilizar las voces de adultos mayores para entrenar modelos de IA.
El segundo, obligar a las plataformas digitales a detectar y sancionar el odio contra los hablantes de lenguas indígenas; y el tercero, financiar a artesanos, creadores y maestros para que puedan comercializar y transmitir, mediante la tecnología, sus conocimientos y oficios en sus propias lenguas.
Cerró su intervención con una invitación a visitar su tierra, la Mixteca Alta, conocer su cultura, probar su gastronomía y admirar y comprar su arte, desde huipiles hasta sarapes, pero “sin regatear”. Enfatizó que se debe preservar el conocimiento ancestral de los pueblos indígenas, empezando por sus lenguas.
“Nos dijeron que nuestras lenguas no cabían en un libro, y sobrevivimos. Hoy nos dicen que no caben en el Internet. Nos quieren borrar de la nube digital, pero se equivocan: ¡porque nosotros ya somos de la nube! No por nada, nuestros hermanos mexicas nos llamaron mixtecos, que en náhuatl significa ‘gente de las nubes’. Somos hijos del ñuu savi, gente de la lluvia. ¡Venimos de la nube y la nube no se le puede borrar ni esconder!”, concluyó.

items.summary: Al filo de padecer Alzheimer, Emilia sueña con volver a ver a su hijo, quien se marchó a Estados Unidos hace 30 años. Un 24 de junio, día de San Juan, la tierra que entraña su origen y el de sus ancestros, hará posible su encuentro. La enfermedad, la vejez, la migración y la niñez son los temas que dan forma a Sókó, primer largometraje de Nicolás Rojas Sánchez (San Juan Mixtepec, Oaxaca, 1984). El cineasta cuenta con cinco cortometrajes, entre documental, ficción y experimental.

items.title: Javier Aranda Luna: El gimnasio bíblico de Monsiváis
items.summary: Hay una paradoja magnética en la biografía intelectual de Carlos Monsiváis. El cronista insomne de la Ciudad de México, el crítico feroz del poder político, el gozoso y falso ateo que diseccionaba la iconosfera y la cultura popular, aprendió a leer –y a debatir– en el seno de una cultura protestante. Antes de ser el gran exégeta de la urbe, el jubiloso hermeneuta del cine, el minucioso cirujano que diseccionó las entretelas de la clase política, fue un niño que empuñaba la Biblia como una espada
