items.body_text:
‘Feminism Is the Consequence of the “Man Problem,” Not Its Cause’
Readers respond to our June 2026 cover story and more.
The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote
Helen Lewis’s “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote” is the most important thing I have read this year. My husband has said that Kamala Harris lost the 2024 election because of the misogyny that exists in America; Lewis’s article proved him correct, with just a teaspoon of humor mixed into an otherwise very frightening topic.
Amy Crist
 Gettysburg, Pa.
Upon finishing “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote,” I found myself equal parts stunned and galvanized. Lewis has an extraordinary ability to illuminate what so many of us feel but struggle to articulate, and this article was no exception.
The MAGA movement contends that feminism is to blame for American decline. But feminism didn’t emerge from nothing. Feminism is the consequence of the “man problem” Lewis identifies, not its cause.
The Bible passage that anti-feminist commentators love to cite is from Ephesians: “Wives, submit to your husbands.” But that’s where they stop reading. The verse goes on to say that a husband must provide for his wife, and love her as he loves his own body. This is not a “do as I say or else” arrangement; it is a covenant of mutual care—her health and happiness are meant to be as important to him as his own, and vice versa. When men forget the instruction to care for their wives as they care for themselves, women have no choice but to learn to care for themselves.
I was recently at the pharmacy, and the man ahead of me—trying to pick up a prescription for his sick wife—answered the pharmacist’s questions with “I don’t know; my wife takes care of that.” When a husband utters, “My wife takes care of that,” the word that means “everything.” It means knowing the passwords, the medications and dosages, the appointment schedules. It means knowing what to say to assuage a teenager’s broken heart, whom to call at the school, how to manage a crisis. It means caring for sick husbands and aging parents—sacrificing for the people you love.
I am the breadwinner in my family. My husband stayed home and raised our three daughters. The plan was for him to return to work once the girls were in elementary school. But we all know what happens when we make plans—God laughs. My husband now lives with a neurological condition that complicates our lives in ways neither of us anticipated. Does working to provide health care for my children and husband make me less of a woman? Would my husband be mocked in the manosphere for not working? Is staying home to raise children noble only when a woman does it?
Erika Jackson
 Gilbert, Ariz.
I worry that “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote” misses a crucial component of the rise of masculinism. I stand in vocal opposition to misogyny and the idiocy of the far-right masculine media sphere. I teach my daughters that they control their bodies and that they should never miss a vote. But I do think that a large cohort of men is struggling with issues that have been ignored, or sometimes even mocked, by the mainstream media. Many men try to be good husbands and parents, only to hear mantras like “We don’t need men” and “There are no good men out there”; on social media, people discuss whether they’d prefer to be trapped in the woods with a man or a bear. Meanwhile, American men are nearly four times more likely than women to die by suicide. The manosphere discusses that issue frequently, as Lewis notes; the mainstream media do not. When men hear negative messages about being a man from the mainstream media but see the manosphere addressing their struggles, they will gravitate toward it. I hope society can learn to address male issues without mocking them. Otherwise, I fear, the extremism will continue.
Ben Rodriguez
 Suffield, Conn.

items.title: Jared Kushner’s Dollar Diplomacy
items.summary: Donald Trump’s son-in-law represents the kind of Washington figure for whom public office serves as a means to extraordinary wealth.
items.body_text:
In the waning hours before the U.S. went to war with Iran, this February, Jared Kushner held a meeting with Iranian negotiators in Geneva—one last chance to avoid a conflict that would plunge the region into chaos and shock the world economy. Afterward, Kushner dismissed his counterparts as unworthy of his time. “Lots of tricks,” he told reporters. “They’re basically playing games with us all over the place, and it’s very, very slippery.”
Kushner, the boyish-looking son-in-law of Donald Trump, has been given an extraordinary brief in recent years. Along with Steve Witkoff, the President’s special envoy, he has been charged with ending wars in Gaza, Ukraine, and just about anywhere else they might break out. Kushner, who is forty-five, has little regard for the craft of diplomacy. In his view, it is less important to know a region’s history or the details of the partisans’ negotiating positions than to simply hear the sides out and split the difference. Peace deals are like real-estate deals, he has said. Both involve hard bargaining and, at times, bluffing. The fact that so many diplomats before him have struggled is a testament not to the intransigence of international problems but to the mediocrity of his predecessors. “I’ve been getting criticized for the last couple of years, by all the people who have tried and failed, for not doing this the same way that they have,” he said in 2020, after Trump unveiled his first Middle East peace plan. “If somebody was successful, I wouldn’t be dealing with this.”
When Kushner and Witkoff began meeting with the Iranian negotiators, in February, the two countries were on the brink of war. In 2025, American and Israeli forces had bombed Iran’s nuclear-enrichment facilities, which Western leaders said were engaged in a decades-long drive to develop a nuclear weapon. Afterward, Trump declared that Iran’s capability to enrich uranium had been “obliterated.” (When the head of America’s top military-intelligence agency disputed the President’s assessment, he was fired.)
Yet Trump and other Western officials wanted further concessions. The Iranians maintained a large stockpile of lower-grade uranium. It was buried under rubble from the bombing in 2025, but Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister, insisted that the Iranians give it up and forswear any intention of enriching uranium in the future. Trump sent Kushner and Witkoff to present the Iranians with what amounted to a binary choice: turn over their entire stockpile or expect an attack. To emphasize his threats, he had dispatched an armada to the Middle East. “We have to have a meaningful deal, otherwise bad things happen,” he said.
Discussions about limiting Iran’s nuclear program are formidably complex, with challenges that are both technical (determining the speeds of centrifuges that can be used) and diplomatic (verifying the Iranians’ often dubious claims of disarmament). But neither Kushner nor Witkoff brought a technical adviser to the talks; though an expert from the Department of Energy had been assigned to Witkoff, he wasn’t in the room. (The White House denied this.) As if to demonstrate their confidence, he and Witkoff were simultaneously negotiating with Russian representatives about the war in Ukraine. The Iran discussions took place in the morning, the Ukraine talks in the afternoon.
A former diplomat briefed on the talks with Iran told me that, when the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, began offering concessions, the two Americans failed to grasp precisely what was on the table. They sought advice from Rafael Grossi, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency, but Grossi was attending the talks as a neutral party. A former White House official who worked on the Iranian nuclear issue was aghast at the lack of preparation: “The Iranians come to you with a proposal. What does it actually mean? items.title: The American Religion of Self-Storage Facilities
items.summary: Why are we so obsessed with putting our belongings in metal boxes and then never looking at them again?
items.body_text:
During the summer of 2019, not long before COVID shut the country down, I spent three and a half days driving from Connecticut, where I live, to Kansas City, where I grew up, and three and a half days driving back. My routes in both directions were lazy and circuitous, and they included not even one mile of interstate highway. I ate roast turkey with all the trimmings at a restaurant in upstate New York that offers Thanksgiving dinner every day of the year; stood at the northern end of a puddle representing the Dead Sea in a grassy park created, a century and a half ago, as a walk-over relief map of the Holy Land; saw surprisingly many sex-toy superstores near billboards promoting belief in Jesus Christ; and visited the birthplace of the Western novelist Zane Grey, who, it turns out, was also a minor-league baseball player and a practicing dentist, and whose real first name was Pearl. Mainly, though, I spent long hours alone in my car thinking about our remarkable country. By the time I got home, I had concluded, based on a multitude of examples, that the two great pillars of American culture are church and self-storage.
A self-storage facility is a business that rents lockable space to people who own more stuff than they know what to do with. (A 2022 survey by the Craftsman tool division of Stanley Black & Decker found that more than a third of the country’s residential garages were so full of overflow possessions that their owners were unable to park cars in them.) “The history of self-storage probably goes back a long way, but the seventies is when it really got started, mostly with mom-and-pop-type operations,” Patrick Lemp, an appraiser and broker who focusses on the industry, told me. “Later, it became an accepted institutional-quality asset class.”
The United States is the world leader, with roughly ninety per cent of global capacity. Texas, of the fifty states, has the most facilities, Hawaii the fewest. Among cities, New York ranks third, after Dallas-Fort Worth and Houston, although on a per-capita basis many smaller municipalities are comparably served. Reno, Nevada, is home to a number of operations that pick up, store, and redeliver tents, chairs, bicycles, and other gear for repeat Burning Man attendees, and Wichita, Kansas, was once named the Self-Storage Capital of the U.S. Units range from closet-size to cavernous, including spaces that are large enough to hold entire houses. Most of the facilities I saw on my road trip were single-story structures with lots of closely spaced roll-up metal doors; some, owned or operated by national chains such as Public Storage, Extra Space Storage, and CubeSmart, looked like office buildings. According to the co-founder and C.E.O. of Neighbor, an industry marketplace that works like Airbnb, there are more self-storage facilities in the U.S. than there are Starbucks, McDonald’s, Walmart, Home Depot, Domino’s, Dunkin’, and Costco locations combined. Annual revenues are estimated to be more than forty billion dollars.
People who work in self-storage often say that their market is driven by “the four D’s”: death, displacement, divorce, and downsizing, all life events that entail sudden collisions between stuff accumulation and reality. Years ago, Paul Roossin, an A.I. technologist and former neuroscientist, moved from a house in the suburbs to an apartment in Manhattan, and, because he thought he might want to move back to the suburbs someday, he rented a twenty-by-forty-foot storage space in Queens, for things that he no longer had room for. The facility was accessible by subway, and he visited from time to time. “Literally, though, years would pass,” he told me. Among the items he stored were a synthesizer, a piano, and a Hammond organ. items.title: She Made Me Do It
items.summary: A prominent dressage trainer shot a belligerent student—and now maintains that he’s the real victim.
items.body_text:
Until 2019, when he attempted to kill one of his students, Michael Barisone was a leading rider and trainer in the horse-handling sport of dressage. Today, he still owns a dressage farm in Loxahatchee, Florida, twenty miles inland from Palm Beach. This part of the state, drained by a grid of canals and centered on the village of Wellington, is the winter capital of America’s equestrian world. Barisone’s operation is relatively modest: there’s no high hedge, no entrance arch. On five acres, he has a stucco house that’s connected to a barn; white-fenced paddocks shaded by palms; and an outdoor riding ring. Along one end of the ring is a common neighborhood fixture: an eighty-foot-long mirror. Barisone, who’s in his early sixties, with a big Will Ferrell chin and a muscular build, can hold a conversation about his own good judgment, and the iniquity of his enemies, while riding a horse and monitoring his own reflection.
In dressage competitions, horses follow a short sequence of bouncing walks and trots, pirouettes and figures-of-eight. It’s an exhibition of control. A horse should do as it’s asked, in a way that projects noble interspecies harmony. Although dressage people have sometimes hoped to broaden their sport’s appeal by calling it “horse dancing,” that may create false expectations. In dressage’s usual form, one discrete movement follows another in a compulsory sequence. There may be a kind of flow, but there’s no sustained rhythm. Competitive dressage less resembles dancing than it does a D.M.V. road test—or floor exercises, if every gymnast had to do the same thing.
Barisone learned dressage during a middle-class childhood in far-upstate New York, and soon excelled at it. In the first of several meetings that I had with him last winter, in Loxahatchee and in New Jersey, he said that, given his ability, he “should have” competed in ten Olympic Games, going back to the eighties. It’s easy to sympathize with an athlete’s disappointments, but Barisone’s narrative of near-misses spans decades. He did represent the United States at the Beijing Olympics, in 2008, as the designated backup for a three-person team. He didn’t ride.
But when Barisone proposed to me that for twenty years he was the dressage equivalent of a major-league-baseball player, that seemed fair—with the caveats that there’s no league and no real audience. He competed at a high level; his income derived from selling horses he’d trained, and from coaching amateur dressage enthusiasts—his “ladies,” as he tends to call them—and their horses, along with a handful of Olympic-level professionals. Barisone and his former wife Vera Kessels followed the migration patterns of their people. They spent winters in Loxahatchee and summers at their other farm—since vacated—in western New Jersey. Barisone sat on dressage-world committees; he was, he told me, a “revered” member of the dressage community. In a 2012 episode of “The Colbert Report,” Stephen Colbert was shown riding in breeches and tails while Barisone, holding a whip, walked alongside him. Colbert’s horse was persuaded to piaffe—to trot in place, knees up, in a way that’s required in advanced dressage competitions. Barisone recently proposed that he was, at that moment, “the most famous horseman in the country.”
In Barisone’s Loxahatchee kitchen there is a dark-green safe the size of a vending machine. It used to stand in his office on the New Jersey farm. He has never seriously contested the idea that, on August 7, 2019, he took a handgun from the safe and drove a few hundred yards, to a house on his property where Lauren Kanarek, a thirty-eight-year-old student of his, was boarding with her boyfriend. He shot her twice.

items.summary: Officials are set to gather in Brussels this week amid growing calls for regulation, including from key figures in the tech industry.
items.body_text:
Government officials from across the European Union will gather in Brussels on Thursday to discuss how to set global rules to counter the threat from new AI models, according to two EU diplomats and a draft agenda seen by POLITICO.
The European Commission will give "updates on EU and international AI policy" and give a "technical briefing on recent AI incidents" during a gathering of the Artificial Intelligence Board, which comprises of representatives from every EU member country and regularly convenes to monitor progress on the bloc's Artificial Intelligence Act.
This week's gathering follows a series of calls to slow down AI development by top company leaders such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman. U.S. President Trump immediately rebuffed the calls, calling the AI safety warnings a "hoax" and arguing that slowing down would give China the momentum in AI.

The alert comes as the WTO struggles to reform itself in a period of heightened global pressure in geopolitics and industrial policy, plus U.S. tariffs.
The WTO’s annual trade report compares three alternative futures for trade cooperation: enhanced cooperation, geopolitical fragmentation, and a world where the WTO is replaced by a network of bilateral and regional free trade deals.

“Materials were found in several places along tracks that were deliberately placed there. This is causing section failures. It seems to be sabotage,” ProRail, the county’s rail infrastructure operator, said in a statement.

items.title: Banking scandal rocks Brazil’s politics and the country’s presidential election in October
items.summary: After ten months of investigation, the Banco Master case points to banker Daniel Vorcaro managing to take the country’s political system hostage.
items.body_text:
On the night of November 17 2025, Brazilian federal agents pulled banker Daniel Vorcaro off the tarmac at Sao Paulo’s Guarulhos airport as he prepared to board a private jet. He was initially detained as a flight risk and arrested a few months later on multiple charges of bank fraud, corruption and money laundering. He currently awaits judgment.
Now, less than a month before Brazil’s national elections, the so called “Banco Master crisis” threatens to shake the country’s democracy to its core.
At first glance, it was just a financial scandal. Soon after Vorcaro’s detention, Brazil’s Central Bank ordered the liquidation of his bank, Banco Master, at an unprecedented loss estimated at R$ 47.3 billion (some US$9.5 billion). Around 90% of this sum was paid back to account holders and shareholders by the Credit Guarantee Fund (FGC) – the Brazilian equivalent of United State’s Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) – the largest payout in the institution’s history.
Brazil’s financial system was put under strain. Since 2018, Banco Master had signed contracts to manage and provide services to state and municipal retirement accounts and banking institutions. Although Vorcaro, if found guilty, would hardly become the first Brazilian scammer in a banker’s suit, investigations have shown that his methods were as creative as they were brutal.
To shield Master’s operations from public scrutiny, Vorcaro has allegedly built a massive network of economists, influencers, bureaucrats, politicians and judges. Some were hired to vouch for the bank, others were, according to prosecutors, openly bribed to allow shady transactions to take place. Whenever the strategy failed, he would allegedly intimidate and blackmail detractors, including journalists and officials, going as far as to plan to harm them physically.
After ten months of investigations, the Banco Master case points to Vorcaro managing to take the country’s political system hostage. The banker seemingly figured out that Brazil no longer had three branches of government that check one another, but three separately purchasable veto points.
Buying access to all three branches of government allowed Vorcaro to hedge against the state. But he could only pull that off because Brazilian politics had become increasingly dysfunctional over the previous decade.
Brazil’s institutional tug of war
In Brazil, Congress executes the budget as much as it legislates. The Supreme Court legislates whenever lawmakers are at a standstill – at times overturning congressional decisions. A weakened president, drowned in public debt and pressured by the other branches, has little leverage to push policy forward. This tug of war has become a trademark of contemporary Brazilian politics.
Legislative aggrandizement harkens back to 2016. During then-President Dilma Rousseff’s impeachment trial, then-Speaker of the House Eduardo Cunha discovered that the speakership could be converted from a procedural office into a sword hanging over the presidency. Congressional earmarks became mandatory and rose from R$ 12.9 billion ($2.5 billion) in 2017 to R$ 61 billion ($12 billion) in 2026 – roughly a quarter of all discretionary federal spending. A president can no longer withhold them to discipline a coalition.
Judicial activism ramped up during President Jair Bolsonaro’s administration. The now jailed former president’s permanent conflict with the Supreme Court over pandemic policy, disinformation and freedom of speech rights pushed justices into a political role they have never relinquished. items.title: African Union peacekeeping is growing as UN missions decline: research finds a mixed record of success
items.summary: At a time when UN peace operations are declining, African organisations are often the first responders to emerging crises.
items.body_text:
When violent conflict erupts in Africa, attention often turns to the United Nations, major powers, or external donors. Yet over the past two decades, the African Union (AU) has become one of the continent’s most important peace and security actors.
From Burundi and Sudan to Somalia, Mali and the Central African Republic, the AU and regional African organisations have deployed peace operations, mediated conflicts, monitored elections and supported political transitions.
These interventions reflect a broader ambition that Africans should play a leading role in addressing Africa’s peace and security challenges.
Despite the growing importance of these interventions, surprisingly little effort has been made to assess what’s been learned from the expanding research scholarship on them.
We are researchers interested in AU peace and security interventions. In a recent scoping review of 186 peer-reviewed articles published between 2000 and 2026, we examined four major themes in the literature:
- AU approaches to peace and security intervention
- legitimacy of AU interventions, particularly among local populations
- effectiveness of AU intervention in achieving long term peace and security
- ownership of AU intervention both at the institutional level and among local populations.
We conclude from the review that debates about AU interventions are often framed too narrowly. Some accounts celebrate African agency and present AU interventions as a clear alternative to external intervention. Others emphasise dependence, limited capacity and operational failures.
The evidence suggests the reality is more complex. AU peace and security interventions are neither clear success stories nor simple cases of dependence on external support. Instead, they show how African actors are increasingly shaping responses to conflict while working with international partners.
The findings reveal both the promise and the limitations of AU peace and security interventions.
From non-intervention to non-indifference
The AU emerged in 2002 from the former Organisation of African Unity (OAU), an institution often criticised for reluctance to interfere in atrocities and armed conflicts.
The new AU argued that sovereignty came with responsibility. Article 4(h) of the AU Constitutive Act gives it the right to intervene in member states in cases of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The result has been far more intervention than before. Over the past two decades, the AU and regional bodies have deployed at least 28 missions to help manage conflicts, support peace processes and improve security.
Legitimacy
The papers we analysed showed that many people regard AU interventions as legitimate because they are “African solutions to African problems”. It reflects a belief that Africans are responsible for managing the continent’s security challenges.
This legitimacy is not merely symbolic. Research suggests that African mediators and peace operations often benefit from being closer to the situation than external actors are.
In some contexts, research shows that shared experiences can make local actors more willing to engage with African-led initiatives.
Effectiveness
The reviewed evidence shows that AU interventions have become more important because they provide practical responses to the continent’s security challenges.
Our research shows that, at a time when UN peace operations are declining and international attention is shifting elsewhere, African organisations are often the first responders to emerging crises.
AU missions have gone where external actors were reluctant to intervene because conflicts were still active. Examples include Somalia and Sudan.

items.title: Physicists zoom into the birth of cosmic rainstorms with new CERN study
items.summary: Scientists recreated cosmic rays in a massive underground particle collider.
items.body_text:
Every second, particles zip through your body at nearly the speed of light. They rain down from a storm high in the sky, where cosmic rays, a powerful type of interstellar matter, are constantly striking atoms in Earth’s atmosphere. The impacts break them apart into a shower of particles that rain to the ground.
Scientists have studied these cosmic rainstorms for over a century, but they lack a precise understanding of how they form. Many researchers are searching for a clearer picture, and they don’t even need to look to the sky to study them. They can instead use a particle collider, CERN’s Large Hadron Collider in Switzerland.
With a team of particle physicists, I study how these cosmic rainstorms are born. We used the world’s first laboratory collisions of oxygen atoms with protons to simulate cosmic rays in the lab. Our results are now published in Physical Review Letters.
What are cosmic rays?
In the early 20th century, physicist Victor Hess discovered cosmic rays aboard hot air balloons. While ascending several kilometers, his instruments found radiation levels unexpectedly kept rising. He deduced these rays must come from space and received the 1936 Nobel Prize in physics for this discovery.
The surprises did not stop there. Experiments later found this cosmic radiation harbored new kinds of matter called antimatter. These new kinds of matter included muons, pions and kaons. These particles are similar to the electrons, protons and neutrons inside atoms, but they exist fleetingly and are harder to see. These building blocks of matter helped fill out the modern theory of particle physics.
Today, scientists understand cosmic rays as fast-moving nuclei – the heavy centers of atoms – from mostly hydrogen. But open questions remain. Where do they come from? How do they reach such high energies?
Scientists are uncovering clues that suggest cosmic rays come from extremely hot and faraway areas of the universe, ejected by exploding stars and powerful objects called supermassive black holes.
Cosmic rays are also helpful for other fields. In the 1950s, scientists discovered they could use them for carbon dating of ancient artifacts, revolutionizing archaeology. More recently, cosmic rays have helped geologists see hidden chambers of active volcanoes, and archaeologists use them to reveal hidden tombs in ancient Egyptian pyramids. This imaging works by measuring how rock deflects the cosmic particles flying at these objects.
How are cosmic showers born?
The usual way to study cosmic rainstorms is by placing hundreds of specialized cameras across several miles of land. Together, these cameras act as one telescope. One of the biggest is the Telescope Array project in the high desert of Utah. This experiment sees the highest energy particles from the cosmos.
To decode information about the cosmic matter bombarding Earth, scientists must use computers to simulate the rainstorm of particles in air. But there is a long-standing problem: Different computer models vary in their predictions for how particle showers form in the sky.
Scientists need to know which model, if any, describes real collisions in the sky. To find out, they need data. No previous experiment has zoomed into the birth of these particle showers, so for several years I collaborated with physicist Lydia Beresford to make the case for reconfiguring our existing instruments at the CERN particle collider to study cosmic rays.
Oxygen beams to recreate cosmic rays in the lab
On July 1, 2025, scientists at CERN pioneered this experiment. They made oxygen atoms collide with protons for the first time using the Large Hadron Collider, the most powerful particle accelerator in the world. For a few days, they recreated cosmic rainstorms in the lab.

Palestinian citizens of Israel mobilise against settler outpost in Galilee
Palestinian citizens of Israel have begun daily protests against an outpost established by settlers from the occupied West Bank in the heart of a Palestinian-majority town in the Galilee.
A group of Israelis reportedly from the Tekoa settlement near Bethlehem set up tents on state land in Majd al-Krum, in northern Israel, on Friday.
The town is home mostly to Palestinian citizens of Israel.
The outpost was established after Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich announced an election campaign plan to “Judaise” the Negev and Galilee by bringing one million additional Jewish residents to the areas.
Smotrich said he wanted to extend the settlement “revolution” from the occupied West Bank to areas inside Israel, where most Palestinian citizens of Israel live.
Majd al-Krum’s local council said the outpost had emerged within “a dangerous political context” and warned that it was intended to create a new reality on the ground.
Izz al-Din Badran, an activist with Majd al-Krum’s popular committee, said residents discovered the outpost on Friday.
The committee subsequently called on residents to maintain an ongoing mobilisation to push the settlers out.

Over 130 lawyers warn UK sanctions on Israeli settlements don't go far enough
More than 130 lawyers, former judges and legal academics have warned British Prime Minister Andy Burnham that sanctions announced last week by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband against Israeli settlements fail to meet the UK’s obligations under international law.
In a six-page letter sent to Burnham on Tuesday, the lawyers welcome the government’s decision to act alongside Canada and France, but state that “the action covered in the recent announcement falls far short” of Britain’s obligations to oppose Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory under a 2024 International Court of Justice ruling.
As part of last week’s announcement, the UK declared that the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory was illegal. Miliband told parliament that he agrees ethnic cleansing of Palestinians is taking place in the West Bank.
Government sources confirmed to MEE that Israeli settlements in the Golan Heights and in East Jerusalem will be also covered by the UK's new measures, as well as those in the occupied West Bank.
Eleven other countries - Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden - joined the UK in supporting or considering sanctions on trade in goods with settlements.

items.title: Hundreds in DRC protest against constitutional amendment for 3rd presidential term
items.summary: Hundreds of protestors gather in the Democratic Republic of Congo's capital Kinshasa to voice their opposition against a government-proposed constitutional amendment
items.body_text:
Democratic Republic of Congo
Hundreds of protestors gathered in the Democratic Republic of Congo's capital, Kinshasa, to voice their opposition to a government-proposed constitutional amendment that could allow President Felix Tshisekedi -- elected in 2019, then re-elected in 2023 -- to stand for a third term following a referendum.
Organised by the C64 coalition, the opposition is calling on President Felix Tshisekedi to "give up" proposed constitutional changes that could open the way for him to secure a third term.
Elections are two years away but tensions are already high between the government and its opponents since the ruling-party-majority parliament approved a proposal to extend the presidential mandate.
Authorities suppressed a July rally in Kinshasa against the constitutional amendment and several opposition supporters were injured in clashes in which the UN said at least one person was killed.
In mid-July, Kinshasa also announced the organisation of a national dialogue long demanded by the opposition, without specifying its terms.
The proposed constitutional change comes as much of the country is riven by conflict, particularly to the east, where the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group seized swathes of territory last year.
items.normalised_title: hundreds in drc protest against constitutional amendment for 3rd presidential term

items.title: DRC: Copper price rises 0.51% on international markets
items.summary: The price of a tonne of copper had also risen during the week of September 7–12, 2026, reaching $14,461.25, compared with $14,350.20 the previous week, an increase of 0.77% per tonne.
items.body_text:
Democratic Republic of Congo
The price of copper has risen by 0.51% on international markets, reaching $14,535.25 per tonne, compared with $14,461.25 the previous week.
A large share of the minerals used to manufacture high-tech products comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The price of a tonne of copper, one of the Democratic Republic of Congo’s key export commodities, increased by 0.51% on international markets, trading at $14,535.25 on September 14, 2026, compared with $14,461.25 the previous week, according to foreign trade price data released Monday.
“The price of a tonne of copper increased on international markets during the period from September 14 to 19, 2026.
The mineral is trading at $14,535.25 per tonne during the week under review, compared with $14,461.25 the previous week, representing an increase of 0.51% per tonne,” the data said.
Compared with the week of August 24–29, 2026, the price of a tonne of copper also increased on international markets.
The mineral traded at $14,437.50 that week, compared with $14,356.20 the previous week, representing an increase of 0.56% per tonne.
The price of a tonne of copper had also risen during the week of September 7–12, 2026, reaching $14,461.25, compared with $14,350.20 the previous week, an increase of 0.77% per tonne.
The Democratic Republic of Congo is Africa’s leading copper producer. The country’s mines produced 2.8 million tonnes in 2023, making the DRC the world’s second-largest copper-producing country.

items.title: Robot valet parking at Gatwick Airport promises safer, easier long‑stay car storage
items.summary: London Gatwick Airport is testing car-parking robots, offering secure, automated long-stay parking for most vehicles at a small extra cost.
items.body_text:
Robot valet parking at Gatwick Airport promises safer, easier long‑stay car storage
The robots, developed by French company Stanley Robotics, can park cars with centimetre-level precision. Gatwick says the system can accommodate around 95% of vehicles, although some cars are excluded. Vehicles must weigh no more than 2.6 tonnes, be under 2.3 metres tall, have a wheelbase of less than 3.3 metres and wheels no larger than 21 inches (53,34 centimètres). The parking area is protected by perimeter fencing, floodlighting and 24-hour security patrols, while automatic number plate recognition monitors vehicles entering and leaving the site. Stanley Robotics says the robots are designed to stop if they malfunction, rather than move unpredictably. Some passengers say the service is quick and easy to book, while others have opted for it because of the added security. The service costs around €6 to €12 more (£5 to £10) than standard long-stay parking. When it launched, the service required a minimum stay of five days and was mainly available on weekdays between 9 am and 5 pm. Gatwick says these restrictions will be gradually eased.

items.title: Why Some of Southeast Asia’s Digital Banks are Starting to Scale
items.summary: Can these institutions threaten the entrenched conventional mega-banks that dominate the region’s financial landscape?
items.body_text:
The world of digital banking is an odd place. A digital bank offers the same basic services as a traditional bank – takes deposits, makes loans – but it does it almost entirely online, eliminating much of the overhead required to maintain a network of brick and mortar branches. Digital banks in this context are standalone businesses, as opposed to digital offshoots of existing banks like Jenius in Indonesia or Trust Bank in Singapore. In fact, if the business model can scale, digital banks might pose a serious threat to the entrenched position of conventional mega-banks that dominate Southeast Asia’s financial landscape.
Despite the promise, digital banking has developed unevenly across Southeast Asia. In Vietnam, there are no true digital banks as digital finance platforms must partner with or be a subsidiary of an existing commercial bank. Regulators in Thailand have also moved slowly in getting the first few digital banks up and running and big potential players, like CP Group’s Ascend Bank, have encountered delays. Indonesia sits on the other end of the spectrum, with digital banks backed by major tech and telecom firms seeing take-off, adding billions in customer deposits and rapidly scaling their loan portfolios over the last few years.
Indonesia’s experience provides some clues about when, why and how digital banks can scale. A key consideration is the regulatory environment. A regulatory system that is supportive of digital banks can open the door for new entrants to challenge incumbents and introduce potentially disruptive innovation into existing systems of banking and finance. Indonesian regulators showed an early willingness to allow this, which is not that surprising given there was a larger tech sector boom underway at the time. That boom has deflated somewhat now, although digital banks remain one of the more promising and profitable legacies of the boom.
In countries with more mature banking sectors, like Singapore, regulators have been cautious in growing digital banks, despite approving the first round of full licenses several years ago. MariBank, owned by tech conglomerate Sea, launched in 2022. Because MariBank is integrated into the Sea ecosystem, which includes its enormous e-commerce arm Shopee, it had amassed S$1.9 billion in deposits by 2025. But limited by tight regulatory oversight, MariBank made only S$222 million in loans and posted a S$56 million loss.
GSX bank, a partnership between telecom giant Singtel and online ride-hailing company Grab, tells a similar story with S$1.8 billion in deposits against S$777 million in loans, and a net loss in 2025. In both cases, the majority of their assets are parked with the central bank or in government and corporate bonds. GSX’s Malaysian arm, GX Bank Berhad, has also been slow out of the gate, reporting total assets of $479 million as of 2025 and a loan to deposit ratio of just 25 percent. There are signs, however, that activity may finally be picking up, with loans jumping 76 percent between December 2025 and June 2026.
In addition to permissive regulatory conditions, the scalability of digital banks depends to a large extent on who is backing them and how digital banking services can be integrated into wider existing commercial ecosystems. In particular, companies that have existing customer networks and use big digital platforms, like telecom and e-commerce companies, have an advantage.
In the Philippines, digital banking appears to be down to a two-horse race between Sea (a familiar refrain by now) and local telecom major PLDT. By the end of 2025, Sea’s MariBank Philippines had assets of just over $1 billion, with its loan portfolio growing 64 percent year over year. Maya Bank, in which PLDT is the main shareholder, reported $1.25 billion in assets and saw its loan book jump 86 percent compared to 2024.
This aligns with what we are seeing in Indonesia, where a friendly regulatory environment combined with backing from major tech, telecom and institution

items.title: China Postponed Its Chang’e 7 Lunar Mission. What Does That Mean for Its Space Program?
items.summary: The lack of explanation – or a new launch date – suggests critical challenges, not just bad weather.
items.body_text:
China’s postponement of its Chang’e 7 lunar mission on August 23 came with a curt explanation from the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA): “China’s Chang’e-7 lunar probe does not meet launch conditions, and its launch therefore cannot take place during the planned window this year.” While there is speculation that the Chang’e 7 launch will take place in 2027, the CMSA has not made any official announcement to that effect.
Given that the Chang’e 7 and Long March 5 Y14 were moved to Launch Complex 101 at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in Hainan Province on August 19, the postponement without adequate explanation, just hours before the launch, is a bit of a surprise. Space missions are often postponed and subsequently rescheduled, but given Chang’e 7’s criticality and its strategic importance to China’s long-term lunar goals, the lack of a rescheduled launch date has been perplexing.
To be sure, China’s Chang’e 7 mission is the most consequential of its phased lunar missions, aimed at showcasing novel technologies like digging for lunar ice and addressing key strategic questions: where are the strategically useful resources on the Moon, and what is the operating environment like? The CMSA said that the Chang’e 7 “mission will employ a comprehensive detection approach, which involves orbiting, landing, roving and hopping to conduct environmental and resource surveys of the lunar south pole.”
The Chang’e 7 departs from China’s earlier missions like Chang’e 3 or 4, since its goal is to demonstrate space resource utilization capabilities. The Chang’e 7 mission includes a hopper to support its planned Chang’e 8 mission, which aims to scale the Moon’s surface toward establishing an International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) by 2036. A statement by the China National Space Administration (CNSA) on April 24, 2025 specified that “the Chang’e-8 mission will target the Leibnitz-Beta Plateau near the Lunar South Pole region, working with the earlier Chang’e-7 mission to conduct scientific exploration and in-situ resource utilization experiments. These efforts will lay the groundwork for the future International Lunar Research Station.” Chang’e 8 is planned to launch in 2029.
Clearly, Chang’e 7 is a core part of Phase Four of China’s Lunar missions. Wu Yanhua, the CNSA’s deputy director, stated that “the main goal of the fourth phase is to carry out scientific exploration on the moon’s south pole and set up a fundamental type of lunar scientific research station. The fourth phase will be carried out in three steps, with the Chang’e 6, Chang’e 7, and Chang’e 8 probes being launched before 2030.”
Phase One of China’s lunar program – Chang’e 1 and 2 – focused on the ability to reach and orbit the Moon. Phase Two – Chang’e 3 and 4 – included a soft landing on the lunar surface, including the far side of the Moon and robotic exploration. Phase Three, Chang’e 5, showcased sample return from the Moon’s near side, which consisted of the collection of lunar material and surface ascent, orbital rendezvous and docking, and safe sample return to Earth. Phase Four moves beyond just demonstrations. Chang’e 6 in 2024 successfully collected and returned samples from the Lunar South Pole. Chang’e 7 is supposed to conduct resource assessment and utilization, with Chang’e 8 following to create the basic lunar infrastructure for the ILRS.
Based on the samples brought back by Chang’e 5 and Chang’e 6, the Institute of Geology under the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences (CAGS), in collaboration with the Institute of Geochemistry under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), Jilin University, Shandong University and China University of Geosciences (Beijing), developed a “1:5,000,000-scale Geological Map of the moon [that] marks 13,519 impact craters, 81 impact basins, 14 types of geological structures and 17 rock types, and includes detailed inset maps of the lunar north and south poles.” In 2024, China published a 1:2,500,000-scale high-precision lunar geologica

items.title: North Korea Confirms September 12 Missile Launch Was Joint Firepower Drill
items.summary: The exercise came a day after trilateral Freedom Edge drills ended and as U.S. President Donald Trump continues to seek a new summit with Kim Jong Un.
items.body_text:
North Korea’s state media confirmed Monday that a joint firepower drill by artillery and missile units across the Korean People’s Army took place on September 12, matching the timing of a ballistic missile launch that the South Korean military had detected the same day.
On September 12, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected multiple short-range ballistic missiles launched from the Wonsan area on North Korea’s east coast at around 5:20 a.m. KST Saturday. The missiles flew about 250 kilometers before landing in the ocean to the east of North Korea. The JCS added that its forces were closely monitoring North Korea’s activity under a firm South Korea-U.S. combined defense posture.
Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), one of the North’s state-controlled media, reported on September 14, two days later, that the launch stemmed from a joint firepower attack drill involving subunits from five artillery and missile joint units. The drill incorporated attack drones, a tactical cruise missile, a large-caliber thermal-pressure multiple rocket launcher, and a tactical ballistic missile, the KCNA said.
“It is one of the training tasks prioritized by the army to get familiar with the procedure for the operation of the integrated firepower control system, the systematic component of the strategic weapons combined management system, improve the specialty of the integrated automatic firepower control of various combat systems and increase the efficiency of destroying the targets with concentrated fire,” Director of the Artillery Bureau Yu Chang Son was quoted as saying in the KCNA report.
The launch came a day after South Korea, the United States, and Japan wrapped up Freedom Edge, a five-day trilateral exercise held from September 7 to September 11 to strengthen air, maritime, and cyber coordination against North Korean nuclear and missile threats. North Korea has previously cast both trilateral and South Korea-U.S. drills as provocations. The September 12 drill fits a pattern in which Pyongyang has answered major allied exercises with missile launches almost immediately after they conclude.
The missile test also came as U.S. President Donald Trump has pushed for a new summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, reviving the personal diplomacy that produced three meetings during Trump’s first term but no agreement on Pyongyang’s nuclear program. Trump has discussed meeting Kim during a possible trip to Asia as early as this fall. His aides have weighed a rendezvous around the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, but no formal arrangements have begun.
However, Kim has kept the overture at arm’s length. He did not mention Trump’s outreach when he presided over a Workers’ Party political bureau meeting in late August even as he called for what state media described as “extraordinary responsibility” in carrying out state projects.
Pyongyang’s latest missile launch marked its first ballistic missile test since August 20, when the North fired a barrage of short-range ballistic missiles hours after Trump said he intended to meet Kim later this year. Neither major military exercises nor renewed diplomatic overtures have interrupted the North’s testing tempo this year.
In related developments on September 14, South Korea’s Unification Ministry said it plans to provide Kangdong County Hospital in Pyongyang with 166 types of medical equipment, according to a local media report. The support falls under a health and medical cooperation program aimed at modernizing the North’s rural hospitals, and Kangdong is considered the first completed example of Kim’s push for such facilities. Kim Dae-sik, a legislator with the main opposition People Power Party, who received the document, said the policy of aiding North Korea “while it pursues nuclear weapons” deserved reconsideration.

items.title: Changing the finance minister is easier than making Indonesia investable
items.summary: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has replaced Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa with Suahasil Nazara. It’s easy to change a minister, but harder to prove that the change will deliver what investors actually want. Indonesia enters this transition with Moody’s and Fitch ratings agencies maintaining their investment-grade sovereign ratings while shifting their outlooks to “Negative.” MSCI, […] The post Changing the finance minister is easier than making Indonesia investable appeared first
items.body_text:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has replaced Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa with Suahasil Nazara. It’s easy to change a minister, but harder to prove that the change will deliver what investors actually want.
Indonesia enters this transition with Moody’s and Fitch ratings agencies maintaining their investment-grade sovereign ratings while shifting their outlooks to “Negative.”
MSCI, assessing a different problem, has raised concerns over shareholder transparency, free-float reliability, possible coordinated trading, price formation and broader investability in Indonesia’s equity market.
These are not identical judgments. Moody’s and Fitch assess sovereign creditworthiness; MSCI assesses whether a market remains sufficiently accessible and investable. But the three independent assessments point in the same uncomfortable direction: Indonesia increasingly has something to prove to the world.
To be sure, the country is not short of economic attractions. It offers scale, natural resources, infrastructure demand, industrialization opportunities and a vast domestic market. Nor has foreign capital disappeared: Bank Indonesia continues to report foreign portfolio inflows through 2026.
At the same time, foreign investment illustrates the problem. Capital continues to enter Indonesia, but the headline number only shows that money arrived — it says much less about what those funds came to do.
Indonesia remains highly capable of attracting capital where the underlying asset can outweigh the institutional discount: minerals, downstream processing, infrastructure, protected project economics and access to domestic demand.
An investor can remain uneasy about parts of the policy environment and still want the nickel, the smelter, the concession or the customer base. The harder test is capital that trusts Indonesia itself.
Regional headquarters, R&D mandates, treasury functions, complex manufacturing ecosystems and repeated reinvestment embed capital much more deeply in the country.
Such commitments are harder to reverse and depend more heavily on regulatory predictability, institutional continuity and confidence that today’s operating assumptions will survive tomorrow’s policy decisions.
For investors, uncertainty carries a price. It can raise required returns, shorten investment horizons, depress valuations and increase the premium demanded for long-duration exposure.
That creates an uncomfortable middle ground: Indonesia can remain attractive enough to receive capital while becoming too expensive for the forms of capital that depend most heavily on institutional predictability.
There is a broader pattern here. Indonesia is rarely short of policy announcements, reforms, incentives, institutional changes or personnel moves. The recurring weakness is proving the specific outcome each was meant to produce.
Investment announcements do not establish investment depth. Market reforms do not establish investability. A new finance minister does not establish fiscal credibility. The evidence that matters sits downstream.
That is the standard against which Purbaya’s removal and Suahasil’s appointment should be judged.
Purbaya’s removal does not prove that his policy direction failed. Suahasil’s long tenure inside the Finance Ministry signals continuity and a technocratic record familiar to investors, which may improve expectations.
What follows will determine whether that matters: fiscal execution, deficit management, policy consistency, coordination among economic authorities and regulatory predictability. Indonesia can change the policymaker. It cannot appoint the market’s response.
Moody’s affirmed Indonesia at Baa2 but moved its outlook from Stable to Negative. Fitch affirmed it at BBB and did the same. Neither agency downgraded Indonesia; both signaled that the balance of risk had deteriorated.

items.title: Indonesia’s housing deal with China needs a green clause
items.summary: This week, Maruarar Sirait, Indonesia’s housing minister, spent four hours at the Jakarta residence of China’s ambassador, Wang Lutong, and emerged with the outline of an ambitious plan. China will help Indonesia build large numbers of apartment blocks, known locally as rusun, by investing capital, sharing construction expertise and partnering with Indonesian firms to get […] The post Indonesia’s housing deal with China needs a green clause appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
This week, Maruarar Sirait, Indonesia’s housing minister, spent four hours at the Jakarta residence of China’s ambassador, Wang Lutong, and emerged with the outline of an ambitious plan.
China will help Indonesia build large numbers of apartment blocks, known locally as rusun, by investing capital, sharing construction expertise and partnering with Indonesian firms to get the job done.
Why does Indonesia need the help? The country faces an acute housing shortage: government data show that 9.29 million families — about 12% of all households — lack adequate housing. Construction also drives large-scale employment, since homebuilding supports 183 other industries, from cement to furniture-making.
The two governments have formed a joint team drawn from Indonesia’s housing ministry, the state housing fund Tapera and China’s Ministry of Housing. Its mandate is to determine which land to use, which regulations to follow and which building technology to import.
That last question reportedly remains unresolved, with officials on both sides saying only that any technology must “fit Indonesia’s conditions,” including safety, land and environmental rules.
That open question carries weight. China builds two very different things. On one hand, it manufactures more solar panels, batteries, heat pumps, and electric vehicles than any other country.
On the other, it also erects vast numbers of ordinary concrete buildings that consume enormous energy and generate heavy pollution. Which version of China’s building technology comes to Indonesia will depend on what gets written into this deal—not on chance.
Indonesia has been here before, in a different sector. Its nickel-mining and battery-material industry grew rapidly on the back of Chinese investment, but much of it runs on coal plants built specifically to power those factories. That choice locked in decades of coal use to support a supposedly clean industry: electric-vehicle batteries.
Buildings last even longer than factories. If millions of new homes are built the old way — reliant on heavy concrete and tethered to a coal-powered grid — Indonesia will be locked into that choice for 30 to 50 years, since homes are neither easy nor cheap to retrofit once standing.
There is a simple way to avoid repeating that mistake. As the two governments draft the rules for this housing program, Indonesia should insist on a full package of clean technology that China already produces at scale.
Solar panels should be built into every rooftop from the start, rather than retrofitted later, especially since Indonesia scaled back its rules for selling surplus solar power back to the grid in 2024, and the state power company has been slow to embrace residential solar.
Batteries should be included, too, so that elevators, water pumps and lights keep running during the power cuts still common in many parts of the country. Heat pumps or efficient air conditioners matter too, since cooling accounts for a large share of Indonesia’s electricity use, and better equipment can cut that consumption significantly.
Cleaner cement should replace the conventional kind: standard cement production accounts for a substantial share of the world’s pollution, and China has developed lower-emission methods of making it.
Parking areas should include space and electrical outlets for charging electric motorbikes and cars, built in from day one rather than added years later at greater cost. And new buildings should use water-saving, energy-efficient appliances, which lower both electricity bills and strain on the power grid.
China has good reason to agree to all this. Its factories now produce far more solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles than domestic buyers can absorb, and prices at home have fallen sharply as a result.
Chinese companies are known to be actively hunting for buyers abroad. A guaranteed, government-backed housing program in Indonesia — one of Southeast Asia’s largest markets — is a good deal for them as well.

Among them were the leaders of heavyweights of the Global South such as China, India, Indonesia, […] The post Putin’s diplomacy blitz strategically targeting the Global South appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
Over the past two weeks, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin staged a major diplomatic blitz. Across three events in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Vladivostok in Russia’s Far East and New Delhi, India, as well as a state visit by Vietnam’s leader, he met with some 18 heads of state.
Among them were the leaders of heavyweights of the Global South such as China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia and Turkey, just to name a few.
The Ukraine war certainly featured in these conversations. Russia has recently ramped up its attacks on Ukraine, further fueling some fears in the West that Ukraine could end up losing the war.
Tellingly, however, the main thrust of discussions led by the Russian president had a different focus: fuel, trade and transit.
Here’s why Russia is deepening ties with many partners in the Global South – and what these meetings tell us about the impacts of Western efforts to isolate Putin.
Shoring up fuel and energy
Fuel and energy security is becoming a mutual concern for both Moscow and its partners in the Global South. Ukraine’s deliberate offensive campaign targeting Russia’s oil refining capacity has resulted in noticeable fuel shortages in the country.
It has forced the Russian government to import refined fuel from countries it has traditionally exported to, such as Belarus, Turkey and India.
At the same time, the Kremlin continues to push to expand its energy exports. This includes finalizing the contract to build the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, which intends to deliver 50 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually from Russia to China via Mongolia.
Last week, Russia also signed a deal to establish a new strategic oil reserves hub in Vietnam.
Russia is also expanding cooperation on nuclear power, which was part of the discussion agenda with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Vietnam’s President To Lam (during his state visit to Russia) and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Deeper ties with the Global South
The ongoing sanctions war between Russia and the West has made its economic and trade relations with the Global South pivotal for the country’s survival and future development.
Two friendly interstate bodies, in which Russia plays core roles, are becoming especially important. The first is BRICS, a group of 11 economies including Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.
The BRICS economies now account for about 40% of global GDP. Last year, mutual trade turnover between BRICS member states exceeded US$1 trillion for the first time.
The second is the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). This is a political and security bloc spanning countries in Europe, Asia and the Indo-Pacific. According to Putin, Russia’s trade turnover with the SCO exceeded US$400 billion in 2025.
Overall, Asia accounted for 73.4% of Russia’s trade turnover last year. It’s no surprise that Moscow’s trade links with Asia featured in almost every conversation in Bishkek, Vladivostok and New Delhi.
Bypassing disruption in the Middle East
Despite its friendly ties with Iran, Russia and its clients aren’t immune from the ongoing disruption to transport and trade routes through the Middle East. To mitigate these risks, Russia is actively lobbying two relatively new transcontinental transit networks.
The first is the 7,200-kilometer combined rail-road-maritime International North-South Transport Corridor. This route connects Russia’s Baltic Sea ports with Mumbai in India, via the Caspian Sea and Iran.
Russia reportedly discussed this route with the Indian and Iranian delegations he met with this month.
The second is the 5,600-kilometer maritime Northern Sea Route, which connects Asia’s ice-free ports with Russia’s Arctic ports as part of the Northeast maritime passage across the Arctic Ocean.
In August, Beijing launched commercial operations along this route for the first time.

items.summary: قال ​الرئيس الأمريكي دونالد ترامب ​الإثنين إن ‌هناك "مؤامرة خبيثة" تستهدف الذكاء الاصطناعي ​ومراكز ‌البيانات، وإن ‌الولايات ​المتحدة تمتلك الصلاحية لتنظيم عمل ​شركات ​القطاع ​ومقاضاتها. يأتي ذلك فيما دعا مفوض الأمم المتحدة السامي لحقوق الإنسان فولكر تورك إلى "تحرك طارئ" لكبح تقنيات الذكاء الاصطناعي فائقة التطور، محذرا من أنها تنطوي على "مخاطر غير مسبوقة".

items.summary: عند مصادقة مجلس النواب الإسباني الخميس على مشروع قانون يفتح الباب أمام منح الجنسية الإسبانية لصحراويين وُلدوا بالصحراء الغربية قبل الـ29 من سبتمبر/ أيلول 1977، في خطوة وصفت بأنها تاريخية. هذا القرار يعيد إلى الواجهة إرث إسبانيا الاستعماري في الإقليم، ويثير في الوقت نفسه أسئلة سياسية بشأن تداعياته على علاقاتها مع المغرب. لمناقشة الموضوع، يشارك في الحلقة: من إسبانيا البشير محمد لحسن الباحث في الإعلام بجامعة إشبيلية، ومن المغرب طارق أتلاتي رئيس المركز المغربي للأبحاث والدراسات الاستراتيجية وأستاذ ا

items.summary: تألق محمد البشير بلومي خلال المباراة التي جمعت فريقه هال سيتي بتشيلسي السبت في الدوري الإنكليزي لكرة القدم، إذ سجل هدفين إضافة إلى تمريرة حاسمة، ما مكن ناديه من انتزاع نقطة ثمينة في ستامفورد بريدج. وساهم نجل النجم السابق لمنتخب "محاربي الصحراء" لخضر بلومي -البالغ 24 عاما- في حفاظ هال سيتي على سجله خاليا من الهزائم في أربع مباريات بينها فوز غال على مانشستر يونايتد 2-0.

items.summary: في هذا العدد من النقاش نتطرق إلى تصاعد التوتر بين الحوثيين والسعودية وسط تصاعد التوتر في الخليج واليمن، فيما أُرجئ اجتماع كان مقررا في سلطنة عُمان بين إيران ودول خليجية لبحث مستقبل مضيق هرمز، بالتزامن مع اتهامات متبادلة بين الطلافين بشن هجمات. ضيوف النقاش: إيمان الحمود، صحفية في إذاعة مونت كارلو الدولية. جمال العواضي، مدير الوكالة الدولية للصحافة والدراسات الاستراتيجية.منى صفوان، كاتبة وصحفية .

items.title: Africa’s biggest refinery launches historic public offering
items.summary: Nigeria’s Dangote refinery has launched Africa’s largest IPO to raise $1.6 billion for a major capacity expansion Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Africa’s biggest refinery launches historic public offering
Nigeria’s Dangote refinery has launched a $1.6 billion initial public offering to help finance a major capacity expansion, in a share sale billed as the largest in African history.
The company is offering up to 4.1 billion shares at 525 naira each, according to its prospectus. The offer opened on Monday and will close on October 13, with trading on the Nigerian Exchange expected to begin in November. The minimum application is ten shares, costing 5,250 naira (around $4).
“We are all going to fully share all our prosperity with the people, and that is why we call it the people’s IPO,” Aliko Dangote said at the launch in Lagos.
Andrey Maslov, director of the HSE University Center for African Studies, told RT that the refinery’s expected valuation of roughly twice its construction cost reflects the project’s success. He argues the IPO has been launched at an advantageous time, when record refining margins and global fuel-market turmoil allow Dangote to raise more capital while selling a smaller stake.
The expert also notes that the Dangote Refinery, “the sole domestic fuel producer in a country of over 200 million people who drive more than 5 million vehicles”, has acquired strategic importance for Nigeria after overcoming opposition from foreign oil companies and delays to its commissioning.
“What is particularly noteworthy is that the shares are listing on the Nigerian exchange, with capital to be raised in naira. This speaks to the maturity of the domestic stock market, sets a strong precedent for other ventures, and proves that local capital markets can serve as a viable source of funding,” Maslov said.
A surge in traffic from retail investors seeking to buy the shares briefly disrupted Nigerian investment platforms Bamboo and Cowrywise on Monday, the two companies confirmed. Nigeria’s Securities and Exchange Commission approved the offer but warned investors against buying shares through unauthorized websites and social media accounts.
The roughly $20 billion refinery, Africa’s largest, with a 700,000-barrel-per-day capacity, was inaugurated in May 2023 and began commercial operations in 2024. It has been central to the Nigerian government’s efforts to boost domestic refining and reduce import reliance.
According to the IPO documents, the company expects net proceeds of around 2.11 trillion naira after expenses. The funds will finance part of a $14.3 billion program to double the Lagos facility’s capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day. The expansion will cover processing units, major equipment, utilities and construction work. The remaining costs will be financed through internally generated cash and other sources, with the project targeted for completion by 2030.
Company figures show that the refinery sold 5.35 million metric tons of petroleum products in the first quarter of 2026, with 42.5% exported to markets across Africa, Europe, Asia and the Americas amid global supply disruptions caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran.
As of May, it supplied around 87.6% of Nigeria’s gasoline market. Dangote also plans to build a $17 billion energy complex in the northern Kenyan coastal town of Lamu, including a 700,000-barrel-per-day refinery.

items.title: Former African rivals boost economic ties
items.summary: Algeria and Mali are seeking closer economic cooperation after restoring diplomatic ties following a prolonged rift Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Former African rivals boost economic ties
Algeria and Mali have agreed to deepen economic cooperation, with mining, agriculture, energy and transport among the sectors identified for potential joint projects, the Malian government said on Monday.
The plans were discussed during talks in Bamako between Malian Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maiga and his Algerian counterpart, Sifi Ghrieb. Officials presented investment opportunities in Mali’s gold and lithium industries, as well as rice and cotton production, livestock, agro-industry and financial services. Mali also highlighted export opportunities involving mangoes, sesame and cashew nuts.
Transport and energy were also on the agenda, with the two sides discussing the Trans-Sahara Highway, Air Algerie links and Mali’s energy deficit. Cooperation in higher education could also be expanded to include research, according to the Malian government.
According to Algeria Press Service (APS), Ghrieb said that Algiers was prepared to resume institutional cooperation between the two countries, describing the move as part of efforts to elevate bilateral relations to a “new stage.”
The talks are the latest step in a rapprochement between the two countries following a diplomatic rift. Relations deteriorated sharply in April 2025, when Algeria said it had shot down a Malian surveillance drone for violating its airspace, a claim Bamako disputed. Tensions had already been mounting after Mali withdrew from a 2015 Algerian-brokered peace deal with northern separatist groups and later accused Algiers of supporting armed groups, an allegation Algeria denied.
The neighbors restored diplomatic ties in July, returning their ambassadors and reopening their airspace. Maiga traveled to Algiers in August in the first high-level visit since the dispute, and the two prime ministers have now agreed on arrangements for a forthcoming visit to Algeria by Malian leader Assimi Goita.
Algeria has also moved to restore ties with Mali’s partners in the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), Burkina Faso and Niger. The other two countries had jointly recalled their ambassadors from Algiers during its dispute with Bamako.
The rapprochement has since expanded into security cooperation, with Algeria deploying four Su-30 fighter jets to Niger in late August at Niamey’s request following a failed military mutiny in the capital.

items.title: South Africa seeks deeper economic ties with India
items.summary: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has called for deeper trade and investment ties with India after the BRICS summit in New Delhi Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
South Africa seeks deeper economic ties with India
South Africa wants to deepen trade and investment ties with India in critical minerals, green industrialization, infrastructure, agriculture and the digital economy, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has said.
Ramaphosa made the remarks after attending the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where he stressed that South Africa’s membership of the grouping provided an important platform to build political and economic ties that benefit the country.
In his weekly letter to the nation, Ramaphosa said more than a fifth of South Africa’s trade was with BRICS countries and that the grouping remained an important forum for investment and trade. He added that South Africa had used the opportunity to strengthen business ties between the two countries.
India is South Africa’s fourth-largest trading partner, while more than 150 Indian companies have invested more than $10 billion (R243,7bn) in South Africa, creating employment for more than 18,000 South Africans, the president noted. South African companies including Naspers, FirstRand Bank, Sanlam and Momentum also have significant investments in India.
Ramaphosa said the two countries held a South Africa-India CEOs Roundtable involving leaders from major Indian and South African companies. ”We highlighted various opportunities for investment and partnership in areas such as green industrialisation, critical minerals and beneficiation, infrastructure, agriculture and the digital economy.”
He noted that Indian companies had welcomed the structural transformation taking place in South Africa, including reforms in the energy, logistics, telecommunications and water sectors, as well as changes involving visas and public digital infrastructure.
India’s strengths in pharmaceuticals and health technology could support South Africa’s ambition to expand local production of medicines and vaccines, while its expertise in information technology, financial technology and digital public infrastructure could also support the modernisation of South Africa’s systems and services, Ramaphosa said. At the same time, South Africa’s critical minerals could support India’s growing renewable energy, battery and automotive industries, the president stressed.
South Africa wanted to turn the potential identified during the visit into practical partnerships and is keen to restore direct flights between South Africa and India, as well as to establish closer working relationships between business chambers in the two countries. South Africa also benefited from its wider co-operation within BRICS, Ramaphosa said.
The group had expanded beyond the initial group of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa following a decision taken at the 2023 BRICS Summit in Johannesburg. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are now also members. Together, the countries account for around half of the world’s population and around a quarter of global trade, Ramaphosa stressed.
He said South Africa had deepened co-operation through BRICS in areas including science and technology, research, education and skills development. The country has also accessed development finance through the New Development Bank for major energy, water and transportation infrastructure investments.
Ramaphosa said South Africa could access a $100 billion pool of currency reserves through the BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement in the event of a liquidity crisis. BRICS co-operation also extended to health, science, agriculture and skills development, while sectors outside government, particularly business, also participated in BRICS activities.
”Looking ahead, our priority as South Africa is to continue to use our membership of BRICS to deepen bilateral co-operation and expand trade and investment ties,” Ramaphosa concluded.

items.title: Pope Leo XIV’s “Freedom Under Grace” released in English
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV’s book “Freedom Under Grace” hits bookshelves in English, bringing together his reflections on the legacy of St. Augustine that has shaped his spirituality. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope Leo XIVâs âFreedom Under Graceâ released in English
Vatican News
The English version of Pope Leo XIVâs book âFreedom Under Grace: Reflections on the Spiritual Tradition That Formed Me,â went on sale on Tuesday, September 15, in the US, UK, Australia, and across the Commonwealth.
âFreedom Under Graceâ brings together the Holy Fatherâs reflections on the legacy of St. Augustine that have shaped his spirituality and vision for the world.
In addition to being the first-ever Pope from the Order of Saint Augustine, this book is of special interest to English-language readers, bringing to light the unique insights and perspective of the Churchâs first American Pope whose mother tongue is English.
According to a press release from Penguin Random House, the book containes addresses, homilies, and personal writings from Fr. Robert Prevostâs time as Prior General of the Order of St. Augustine, revealing the âwhyâ behind his contemplative responses.
 The future Pope Leo XIV âinvites readers to sit at the table, as if in real time, responding to the aftermath of 9/11, emerging political ideologies, and the Churchâs response to poverty and human rights conflicts.â
âDrawing from the work of St. Augustine, whom he calls his spiritual father,â notes the press release, Pope Leo âadvances a vision for life rooted in community, solidarity, and service to marginalized communities.â
The English version of âFreedom Under Graceâ is published in the US by Image Books, an imprint of the Penguin Random House Christian Publishing Group.
In the UK and Australia, the book is published by the Enlighten imprint of Penguin Random House UK.
The original Italian was published by the Vatican Publishing House (LEV) under the title âLiberi sotto la Grazia.â
The audiobook edition will feature opening homilies and addresses read by Emmy award-winning comedian and devout Catholic Stephen Colbert, and the main text will be narrated by award-winning narrator and Grammy nominee Scott Brick.
Learn more and order your copy at https://freedomundergrace.com

items.title: Jordan's Crown Prince visits baptism site ahead of 2,000 years since Jesus' Baptism
items.summary: Jordan's Crown Prince Al Hussein bin Abdullah II visits the Baptism Site of Jesus Christ (Bethany Beyond the Jordan) and emphasizes the need to carefully plan for the 2030 millennium celebrations, commemorating two thousand years since the baptism of Jesus Christ. Read all
items.body_text:
Jordan's Crown Prince visits baptism site ahead of 2,000 years since Jesus' Baptism
By Fr. PaweÅ Rytel-Andrianik
The year 2030 will mark 2,000 years since the traditional date of Jesus' baptism by John the Baptist. Bethany Beyond the Jordan â today known as Al-Maghtas â is regarded as the site of Christ's baptism.
Crown Prince Al Hussein bin Abdullah II during his visit to this site on September 13 issued directives to improve the site to enhance the experience of Christian pilgrims and visitors.
"The Crown Prince emphasised the need to carefully plan for the 2030 millennium celebrations, commemorating two thousand years since the baptism of Jesus Christ, in a manner that reflects the profound history of the site and occasion, and reaffirms Jordanâs status as a premier global destination for Christian pilgrimage," read a statement of The Royal Heshemite Court.
âThe Crown Princeâaccompanied by Prince Ghazi bin Muhammad, His Majestyâs chief adviser for religious and cultural affairs and personal envoy, and chairman of the Baptism Site Commissionâs board of trusteesâwas briefed on the services offered to pilgrims and visitors. Her Royal Highness Princess Miriam Ghazi, Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Imad Hijazin, Director of the Office of the Crown Prince Zaid Baqain, and Baptism Site Commission Director General Abdullah Bawareed accompanied the Crown Prince on the visit,â it said.
Crown Prince Al Hussein bin Abdullah II underlined the need to promote the Baptism Site more widely, in coordination with the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Jordan Tourism Board, and all relevant partners.
At Al-Maghtas, in Jordan, archaeological excavations have uncovered the remains of churches, chapels, hermitsâ caves, and a baptistery â places of worship tied to Jesusâ Baptism. In 2015 this area was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
Three Popes have made pilgrimages there: John Paul II, Benedict XVI, and Francis.
