items.title: Pope's Alma Mater reveals first Pope Leo XIV Sustainability Medal recipient
items.summary: At a press conference held in the Sala San Pio X of the Vatican, Villanova University announces that Cardinal Michael Czerny, S.J., was selected as the inaugural recipient of the Pope Leo XIV Sustainability Medal, and reveals new details about the upcoming 2026 Villanova University International Sustainability Conference. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope's Alma Mater reveals first Pope Leo XIV Sustainability Medal recipient
By Deborah Castellano Lubov
 
The winner of the first-ever Pope Leo XIV Sustainability Medal is Cardinal Michael Czerny, S.J., Prefect Emeritus of the Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, in recognition of his decades of "remarkable service" and as "a leader whose life reflects the very best of what this medal represents."
This was revealed by the President of Villanova University, Fr. Peter Donohue, Ph.D., O.S.A. on Monday during a press conference hosted by the university on September 14 in the Vatican's Sala San Pio X, down the street from St. Peter's Square, to announce the inaugural recipient of the Medal.
Alongside the University President at the conference were Cardinal Czerny and Dr. Manuela Priesemuth-Payan, Ph.D., Faculty Director for Ethics and Social Responsibility at Villanova School of Business, and Alessandro Gisotti, Deputy Director Editorial of the Dicastery for Communication, who moderated.
Villanova University is an Augustinian Catholic institution located near Philadelphia in the United States, where Pope Leo XIV, then Robert Prevost, earned a Bachelor of Science in Mathematics in 1977. The University later awarded him an honorary Doctor of Humanities degree in 2014.
Alessandro Gisotti opened the event by recalling that all were gathered on this special day, as September 14 marks the birthday of Pope Leo, reflecting on how it is a gift to be discussing these themes important to him.
Recalling that the Prior General of the Augustinian Order Worldwide, Fr. Joseph Farrell, O.S.A., was in attendance, Mr. Gisotti observed that Fr. Farrell's presence underlines the great Augustinian inspiration behind the events being discussed today.
Fr. Donohue: âmoving from dialogue to meaningful actionâ
Before discussing the Medal itself, Fr. Peter Donohue thanked Pope Leo for his leadership, witness, and steadfastness in working to protect our common home and promote human rights.
He explained that the Pope Leo XIV Sustainability Medal is intended to recognize individuals from any field or discipline whose leadership reflects a holistic approach to sustainability. Laureates are selected for work that integrates care for the environment, social justice, protection of vulnerable communities, and responsible economic stewardship.
Presented every two years during the Villanova University International Sustainability Conference, he said it seeks to inspire leadership, encourage innovation, and promote collaboration in building a more just and sustainable world.
The President of the University went on to highlight that this year's winner was Cardinal Michael Czerny, with his decades of remarkable experience in advancing human dignity, human rights, and environmental stewardship, "reflects the spirit the Medal was meant to honor."
Cardinal Czerny says Medal represents a call to responsibility and action
Cardinal Czerny expressed his gratitude for the honor.
 
âI commend Villanova," he said, "for courage to stand up in this very public way to say we pledge to serve society by preparing people to take real responsibility for the world that is coming into being â and thatâs not just ecology responsibility, but also responsibility for artificial intelligence and more broadly and deeply with political responsibility, where it is always harder to exercise it.â
The Medal, he said, has great significance for the person who receives it, but what is more important here is the donor, the fact that this American university is making such a commitment to sustainability is noteworthy.
âThe Medal challenges us to ask what future we are preparing forâ
Moreover, Cardinal Czerny suggested the Medal symbolizes the challenge for the University to ask itself: "what are we preparing these future graduates for?"
âNow there are very serious questions about the future, and to say we prepare you for the future," the Jesuit Cardinal underscored, "is a very bold promise
